sites.name: 3 Times Square
sites.description:
Built and reimagined by Rudin with architect FXCollaborative, 3 Times Square is a 30-story, Class-A office tower in the heart of Midtown Manhattan. Following an extensive modernization, the property now features a jewel-box lobby, a suite of hospitality-inspired amenities, and workspaces designed for the modern tenant. 

The tour offers a rare look inside an iconic Times Square property and will include the new triple-height lobby, the 16th floor amenity suite, the building’s award-winning engine room, a pre-built marketing office floor, and a raw, white-boxed space for a side-by-side comparison of how tenant spaces are conceived and delivered. The tour will conclude on the building's outdoor terrace offering spectacular views of Midtown Manhattan. 

Rudin, the building's owner and operator, will lead the tour alongside Timothy Sudweeks, principal at FXCollaborative, to offer an operational and architectural perspective.
sites.short: Go inside an iconic Times Square skyscraper with a design tour focused on its remarkable modernization, featuring hospitality-inspired amenities, an award-winning engine room, and panoramic Midtown views from an outdoor terrace.

Visit both floors with Silverstein Properties during OHNY Weekend.

sites.name: 20 Exchange Place
sites.partner: JG Neukomm Architecture and The Dermot Company
sites.description:
Led by Founding Principal Jean-Gabriel Neukomm, AIA, this tour of 20 Exchange Place, one of Lower Manhattan's most distinguished Art Deco towers, presents JG Neukomm Architecture's newly completed renovation of the building's lobby and amenity spaces, and explores how the tower's layered history shaped a design that is quietly contemporary and deeply rooted in place.

Completed in 1931 as the headquarters of the City Bank Farmers Trust Company, the building carries decades of accumulated history that JGNA treated not as backdrop but as active design material. The renovation draws on the tower's original Art Deco vocabulary, featuring an ornate entrance arch, coffered ceilings, and bold geometry, while introducing a palette that feels unmistakably of the present: muted burgundy and navy against quartzite columns, terrazzo floors, and furniture rooted in the interwar design tradition. The tour moves through the lobby, model units, and the 19th-floor amenity suite, which includes a food and beverage lounge, co-working areas, fitness and yoga spaces, a screening room, and a listening and podcast room.

The building's history is richer than its financial origins suggest. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, nearby Coenties Slip was home to a community of artists including Agnes Martin, Ellsworth Kelly, Lenore Tawney, and Jack Youngerman, who found cheap studio space in a neighborhood the rest of Manhattan had written off. That overlooked chapter is woven into the renovation, surfacing in material choices, art selections, and the sensibility of a project that refuses the generic.
sites.short: Explore a newly renovated Art Deco landmark with exclusive access to its lobby, model units, and amenity suite, where original architectural details blend with contemporary design inspired by the building’s layered history and the creative legacy of local artists.

sites.name: 50 Years of Dieu Donne at The Grolier Club
sites.description:
Highlighting revolutions in contemporary American hand papermaking, Pioneers in Hand Papermaking celebrates the 50th anniversary of the Dieu Donné Papermill in New York—a studio where master papermakers work with contemporary artists to develop their imagery in different disciplines. Featuring more than 110 works from the collections of Susan Gosin and the Dieu Donné Archive & Collection, the exhibition includes custom sheets of paper and two- and three-dimensional works by artists such as Michele Oka Doner, William Kentridge, Glenn Ligon, and Richard Tuttle, among others.

Artistic techniques include line and chiaroscuro watermarking, pulp painting, stenciling, and paper casting, with videos that show artists’ reimagination of these processes, alongside papermaking tools and materials. Curated by Dieu Donné co-founder and Grolier Club member Susan Gosin with Cynthia Thompson, Pioneers is the 1,000th exhibition presented at The Grolier Club. An accompanying publication from Chronicle Books will be available at this event, and curator and Dieu Donné co-founder Susan Gosin will be present to answer any questions and converse with visitors.
sites.short: Celebrating Dieu Donné 50th anniversary, Pioneers in Hand Papermaking features over 110 innovative paper artworks. The milestone exhibition—1,000th presented at the Grolier Club—highlights contemporary American papermaking techniques through diverse artistic collaborations and tools.

sites.name: 77 Water Street
sites.description:
77 Water is an existing 26-story, 547,000-square-foot office building in New York City’s Financial District. In one of the most significant office-to-residential conversions currently underway in Lower Manhattan, Vanbarton Group is repositioning the building, transforming it into a luxury residential property with 647 units and 30,000 square feet of amenity space.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors will join a guided tour with CetraRuddy, the architect leading the transformation, and see aspects of the design process rarely visible to the public: how an existing commercial structure is re-massed, how new architectural elements are integrated with the original building, and how its interiors are reshaped to create a distinctly residential experience.

sites.name: 610 Loft & Garden
sites.description:
Situated atop Rockefeller Center, 610 Loft & Garden offers a striking example of how modern architecture and historic context intersect in Midtown Manhattan. The venue combines a sleek, contemporary loft interior with a meticulously landscaped rooftop garden, complete with a reflective pool and sculptural plantings. From this elevated vantage point, visitors can take in one of the city’s most iconic urban juxtapositions: the neo-Gothic spires of St. Patrick’s Cathedral rising directly across Fifth Avenue against the backdrop of Manhattan’s modern skyscrapers.

During OHNY Weekend, guests are invited to explore how the design of 610 Loft & Garden extends Rockefeller Center’s tradition of integrating architecture, art, and public space. The rooftop’s unique perspective highlights the layered history of the city’s built environment, offering a rare opportunity to experience the dialogue between past and present in the heart of New York.
sites.short: Experience a rare opportunity to explore a modern loft and rooftop garden overlooking St. Patrick’s Cathedral, where contemporary design meets historic architecture, offering stunning views and unique insights into the city’s evolving skyline.

sites.name: 620 Loft & Garden
sites.description:
Overlooking Rockefeller Plaza from the top of 620 Fifth Avenue, 620 Loft & Garden offers a rare balance of modern interior space and historic urban views. Its loft-like gallery opens directly onto a landscaped rooftop garden, complete with a reflecting pool and seasonal plantings, creating a quiet retreat above the city’s busiest corridor. From here, visitors enjoy one of New York’s most striking perspectives: the axial view down Rockefeller Plaza, framed by the Art Deco façades of Rockefeller Center and anchored by St. Patrick’s Cathedral across the avenue.

During OHNY Weekend, guests are invited to explore how 620 Loft & Garden contributes to the architectural legacy of Rockefeller Center. The rooftop’s design highlights the complex’s vision of blending architecture, landscape, and city life, while offering a unique vantage point to appreciate the dialogue between Midtown’s historic landmarks and its evolving skyline.
sites.short: Ascend to a rarely accessible rooftop garden and gallery, where you can enjoy sweeping views over Rockefeller Plaza and Midtown’s iconic landmarks while learning how this hidden space blends architecture, landscape, and city life.

sites.name: 1914 Lehigh Valley Railroad Barge
sites.description:
Come visit the historic 1914 Lehigh Valley Barge No. 79, a floating museum & showboat housed aboard the last remaining covered wooden barge that has been lovingly restored and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Discover the history of the Tug and Barge “Lighterage Era” (1860-1960) and how food and commercial goods were transported prior to today’s bridges and tunnels.

The Lehigh Valley No. 79, is a typical unaltered example of the wooden barge construction used from the 1860's to the 1980's in the Port of New York for the railroad lighterage system. Thirteen railroads served the Port and almost all had terminal facilities on the New Jersey shoreline. Because of the lack of railroad tunnels and bridges, goods to be consumed in New York City and cargo to be loaded upon vessels for shipment overseas first had to be transported by water across the Hudson River. To perform this function, various railroad companies maintained large fleets of barges and tugs to move them. The Lehigh Valley Railroad had over five hundred barges of which about 100 had a covered barn-like structure like Barge 79 to keep cargo like grains, coffee, and flour dry and protected. Containerization (1956 to present) made these barges obsolete.
sites.short: Step aboard the last surviving covered wooden barge from New York's “Lighterage Era” to explore exhibits about historic cargo transport and enjoy family-friendly games and storytelling.

sites.name: ABC No Rio
sites.partner: ABC No Rio and Paul A. Castrucci Architects
sites.description:
“ABC No Rio was a vital, dangerous and confrontational art space on the Lower East Side.” John Leland, _The New York Times_

Born from a 1979 break-in of an abandoned building (so punk), ABC No Rio grew into one of New York’s most fiercely independent homes for radical art, activism, and community. For nearly a decade, it’s existed on sheer will without a permanent home, taking its exhibitions, punk matinees, performances, workshops, printmaking, and organizing wherever it could gather.

Now, after years of organizing, fundraising, and fighting to stay alive, ABC No Rio is almost home again, this time in a brand-new four-story building designed to perform as boldly as the organization's mission.

Built using Passive House methodology and high-performance energy strategies, the new center pairs rigorous environmental design with spaces made for art, music, activism, and community. Join ABC No Rio Executive Director Gavin Marcus and architect Paul A. Castrucci for a tour of the building at 156 Rivington Street.

During OHNY Weekend, explore the galleries, performance spaces, artist studios, printshop, darkroom, zine library, digital media lab, communal kitchen, roof garden, and more. Along the way, learn how a highly adaptable cultural program, low-carbon strategies, sustainable materials, and high-performance systems come together to create a building that can support ABC No Rio for generations. Come see the next chapter of ABC No Rio.
sites.short: Tour a revived downtown arts center with access to galleries, studios, printshop, darkroom, zine library, and more, while learning how sustainable design and radical creativity shape its future.

sites.name: Adventure Playground
sites.description:
Perched on a hillside just inside Central Park’s West 67th Street entrance, Adventure Playground is one of the most influential playgrounds ever built in the United States. Opened in 1967 and designed by architect Richard Dattner, it marked a radical departure from the standardized swings, slides, and asphalt play yards that characterized most urban playgrounds of the era. Instead, Dattner created a sculpted landscape of pyramids, tunnels, climbing mounds, mazes, water features, and interconnected structures that encouraged exploration, imagination, and self-directed discovery. Inspired by postwar European adventure playgrounds, the design viewed play not as a prescribed activity but as an act of invention, allowing children to create their own paths, challenges, and experiences. 

More than simply a playground, Adventure Playground represented a new architectural approach to childhood. Dattner studied how children actually played and collaborated with child-development experts to shape an environment that balanced physical challenge with creative freedom. Concrete, granite, wood, water, and topography became tools for exploration, transforming the entire site into a play experience rather than a collection of equipment. 

The playground’s legacy extends far beyond Central Park. It became a seminal example of the adventure-play movement in America and helped establish playground design as a legitimate field of architectural and landscape innovation. Its influence can be seen in generations of designers who increasingly viewed playgrounds as immersive environments that foster social interaction, creativity, risk-taking, and independent learning. Nearly sixty years later, Adventure Playground remains both a beloved destination and a landmark in the evolution of architecture for play. Join this tour for a rare opportunity to hear directly from Richard Dattner as he reflects on the origins of this groundbreaking project, the ideas that shaped it, and its enduring influence on the design of play environments around the world.
sites.short: Explore the groundbreaking design of a pioneering playground with its original architect, Richard Dattner, as he shares insights into its innovative features, creative philosophy, and lasting global impact on play spaces.

sites.name: Alice Austen House
sites.description:
Discover the Alice Austen House, a National Historic Landmark and LGBTQ+ historic site, set within a stunning 15-acre waterfront park with sweeping views of New York Harbor.

OHNY Weekend visitors can participate in a guided tour of the permanent exhibition "New Eyes on Alice Austen" in addition to the museum's Queer Ecologies Garden. Visitors will receive a reflective zine that invites them to see themselves in the plants and nature curated in the garden beds.

Follow shoreline paths and meadows to the park’s overlook, offering an unmatched perspective on the harbor, then step inside the Victorian Gothic cottage museum where pioneering photographer Alice Austen lived and worked for nearly 50 years. The house and its surrounding landscape reveal Austen’s adventurous spirit, her relationship with lifelong partner Gertrude Tate, and the deep connection between place and creativity.

Guests may also rent a Polaroid camera during their walk to create their own keepsake images, a nod to Austen’s passion for photography. Whether visitors come for the art, history, or natural beauty, this experience offers a unique way to explore one of Staten Island’s most storied sites.
sites.short: Explore a landmark cottage and historic LGBTQ+ site on Staten Island, with guided exhibition tours and an interactive photography activity, in a peaceful setting with stunning views of New York Harbor.

Printed materials and low-vision teaching aids are available.

sites.name: Allison Eden Studios
sites.description:
OHNY Weekend offers a rare opportunity to step inside one of New York City’s most celebrated working art studios. Nestled in the heart of Brooklyn, Allison Eden Studios has spent more than three decades transforming ordinary spaces into extraordinary environments through handcrafted stained glass and mirror mosaics commissioned by leading architects, interior designers, luxury hotels, restaurants, museums, and private collectors around the world.

Visitors will experience a behind-the-scenes look at a creative process that is typically closed to the public. Watch master artisans cut, shape, and assemble thousands of pieces of brilliantly colored glass into spectacular works of art. Explore large scale installations in progress, discover the evolution of a design from concept sketch to finished masterpiece, and learn how traditional mosaic craftsmanship is combined with contemporary design and innovative fabrication techniques.

Throughout the studio, guests will encounter an explosion of color, texture, and light while viewing original artworks, architectural installations, and iconic commissions. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet Allison Eden, hear the stories behind her internationally recognized projects, and gain insight into how Brooklyn continues to inspire one of America’s leading mosaic artists. As a proud Brooklyn-based design studio, Allison Eden Studios preserves the tradition of handcrafted American artistry while demonstrating how art can transform architecture, elevate interiors, and bring joy to everyday spaces.
sites.short: Visit a renowned working art studio to watch master artisans create vibrant stained glass and mirror mosaics, explore large-scale installations in progress, and meet the artist behind internationally acclaimed projects.

No strollers allowed inside the studio.

Children ages 10+ are welcome accompanied by an adult.

sites.name: Amant and Zoli
sites.description:
Amant is a center for contemporary art in Brooklyn, housed across a 31,000-square-foot, five-building campus that includes exhibition and performance spaces, a café, bookshop, and restaurant. Zoli, the campus's American, seafood-focused restaurant, was designed by GRT Architects and sits within the Amant grounds. 

OHNY Weekend visitors can tour Amant with Chief Curator Tobi Maier, Curator Patricia Hernandez, and Curatorial Assistant Ariana Kalliga, and tour Zoli with Rustam-Marc Mehta, Founding Partner, and Sophie Nichols, Associate, of GRT Architects, gaining insight into both Amant's approach to exhibiting contemporary art and the design of the restaurant it shares its campus with.
sites.short: Tour contemporary art spaces and a uniquely designed seafood restaurant with curators and architects, gaining insider perspectives on both the art exhibitions and the architectural vision behind the campus.

sites.name: American Academy of Arts and Letters
sites.partner: American Academy of Arts and Letters

address.note: Enter through the Audubon Terrace gate on Broadway between West 155th and 156th Streets, and walk past the Hispanic Society to the far end of the Terrace on the left.

sites.description:
The American Academy of Arts and Letters is an honor society of 300 members (in the departments of Architecture, Art, Literature, and Music) whose mission is to foster and sustain interest in the arts. The founding members met for the first time in New York City in February 1899.

Arts and Letters has occupied its Beaux Arts buildings on Audubon Terrace in Washington Heights since the 1920s. Its original building was designed by member William Mitchell Kendall from McKim, Mead, & White; and a second building was designed by member Cass Gilbert. Construction was funded by writer, historian, and member Archer M. Huntington, who was responsible for the development of Audubon Terrace as a cultural complex. Huntington also founded the neighboring Hispanic Society Museum & Library.

On OHNY Weekend, the Members’ Room and Portrait Gallery will be open to the public. Visitors will also be able to explore Arts and Letters’ fall 2026 exhibitions – a season of collaboration, play, and worldmaking. Christopher Williams opens the first round of _The Game_, a series of interlocking shows staged by artists over the coming year. _Arakawa and Madeline Gins: The Poetic Jump_ surveys the duo’s lifelong collaboration with imaginative, experiential works across media that question “the mistaken concept of the unavoidable death”; and in _Origins _始源, Yoshitaka Amano shows recent drawings and materials from key animation and character design projects.
sites.short: Step inside Beaux Arts spaces rarely open to the public including the Portrait Gallery and Members’ Room and discover exhibitions by contemporary artists at this McKim, Mead, & White and Cass Gilbert-designed cultural campus.

To use the lift, please ring the bell or call (212) 368-5900 to arrange for a staff member to meet you. 

With prior arrangement, visitors using wheelchairs may also enter through the garage to the left of our administrative entrance, located at 633 West 155th Street. There is an elevator, sized 36 inches deep and 34 inches wide, that reaches all levels of the building. Concrete ramps connect our buildings to the Arts and Letters terrace. Please note that the slopes of the garage entrance (14%) and hallway to the elevator (18%) are steeper than the ADA-recommended maximum. Please call (212) 368-5900 or email info@artsandletters.org by October 14 to arrange for a staff member to assist with entry through the garage. 

Visitors may request a wheelchair for on-site use.

sites.name: American Folk Art Museum
sites.description:
The American Folk Art Museum is the nation’s museum of folk and self-taught artists. Candid, genuine, and unexpected, AFAM celebrates the creativity of individuals whose singular talents have been refined largely through personal experience rather than formal artistic training. With a collection spanning 7,500 works of art from four centuries and nearly every continent, the Museum engages people of all backgrounds through its collections, exhibitions, publications, and public programs as the leading forum shaping the understanding and appreciation of folk and self-taught art.

During OHNY Weekend, two exhibitions will be on view. Featuring spectacular examples of needlework and other ornamental arts made by American girls in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, “Locating Girlhood: Place and Identity in Early American “Schoolgirl” Art” sheds new light on a rich but understudied genre, offering one of the most significant presentations on the subject in recent memory. Mounted during the celebration of the United States semiquincentennial, “Folk Nation: Crafting Patriotism in the United States” draws from the American Folk Art Museum’s rich collections to explore links between vernacular art and the construction of an American sense of self.
sites.short: View two exhibitions of American folk and self-taught art made by individuals whose singular talents have been refined largely through personal experience rather than formal artistic training.

sites.name: Andrew Carnegie Mansion: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
sites.description:
Discover the Andrew Carnegie Mansion up close as Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, opens the doors to one of the city’s most captivating Gilded Age homes. Learn about the history of the mansion and its transformation from home to museum. Participants will move through the mansion’s grand and intimate first-floor rooms—spaces shaped by Carnegie’s forward‑looking ideas about home, technology, and design. 

Led by curatorial and conservation staff, visitors will have the rare chance to explore artifacts and personal items connected to the Carnegie Mansion. From plaster molds used for the mansion’s ornamental details to objects tied to the family’s daily life, these materials offer a more personal lens on how the Carnegies lived in—and shaped—this remarkable home. 

This experience brings together architecture, history, and personal stories to the mansion as both a design landmark and a lived space.
sites.short: Go inside one of the city's most fascinating Gilded Age mansions to explore rare artifacts and learn about the building's transformation from home to museum on this guided tour led by curatorial and conservation staff.

ASL interpretation is available by request for any Cooper Hewitt tour or program, free of charge. To request these services or inquire about what services will be provided, email CHAccess@si.edu or call 212.849.2950. Please make your request at least one week prior to your visit.

sites.name: Andy Kessler Skatepark
sites.partner: NYC Skateboard Coalition and Riverside Parks Conservancy

address.note: Enter Riverside Park at 108th Street, then walk down towards the Hudson River.

sites.description:
Originally opened in 1996 as the first full-sized public skatepark in Manhattan, Riverside Skatepark reopened in 2019 and was renamed to honor Andy Kessler, the pioneering New York skateboarder who helped design, fund, and build the original park.

sites.name: Astoria Park Pool
sites.description:
Astoria Pool is one of eleven immense outdoor public pools opened in 1936; a summer which broke local heat records, not unlike today. This heroically scaled pool, the largest in the city to this day, was financed by the Federal Works Progress Administration (WPA) as part of an effort to alleviate adverse health conditions and provide safe recreation for New Yorkers from predominantly working-class communities who frequently swam in often treacherous and polluted rivers and streams. 

Astoria is distinguished by its streamlined and simple forms, decorative glass block, deco-style steel railings, and Art Moderne style ticket booth. When opened it featured separate swimming, diving and wading areas, perimeter bleachers, locker rooms which served as gyms during non-summer months, massive filtration systems, heating units, and even underwater lighting. 

Framed by the Triborough and Hell Gate bridges, the pool accommodated 5,570 bathers on opening day. WPA administrator Harry Hopkins called it “the finest pool in the world.” In 1936 and 1964, the pool hosted the Olympic Trials for the U.S. Swim and Diving Teams. In 2006, Astoria Pool was designated an official New York City landmark. 

Over the past decade, NYC Parks has invested over $30M to restore the multi-level diving board, create a performance plaza, install a new filter system, pool deck, and tub, and create a many-jetted interactive spray feature. On this tour you will view original architectural finishes, visit the massive changing rooms, restrooms, showers, and the state-of-the-art filter plant, a space not open to the public. Tours will be led by Mark A. Focht, PLA, FASLA, First Deputy Commissioner of NYC Parks.
sites.short: Explore the city's largest historic pool, admire original Art Moderne features, and get exclusive access to the restored changing rooms and state-of-the-art filter plant—areas typically closed to the public.

All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Atlantic Yards: A Megaproject Rebooted?
sites.description:
Hugely controversial when proposed in 2003 and later approved, the Atlantic Yards megaproject, renamed Pacific Park Brooklyn in 2014, is at a crossroads as new developers aim to make it viable by adding 37% more apartments in larger towers. 

This tour, led by watchdog journalist (and tour guide) Norman Oder, will explore the history of the Barclays Center, once to be designed by Frank Gehry and later rescued by SHoP, its “accidental” plaza, and the towers that flank it, as well as the project's other extant block with four towers and an initial tranche of open space.

The tour will also discuss the recently proposed plan by the project's new developers to deck an MTA rail yard for five towers and open space, plus the effort to transfer the bulk from Gehry’s unbuilt flagship tower, once slated to loom over the arena, to create a giant two-tower project across Flatbush Avenue.

Learn about Atlantic Yards’ tangled history, unfulfilled affordable housing pledges, changing plans (and owners/designers), and new questions about subsidies, program, and timetable. Topics discussed will include public accountability, open space, arena design/operations, and the changing context in Brooklyn.
sites.short: Join a journalist-led tour of the Brooklyn megaproject, discussing its complex history from its controversial beginnings and evolving designs to current plans for expanded towers, plus ongoing debates over affordable housing, public accountability, and neighborhood impact.

Urban Builders Collaborative (UBC) as the managing member, along with not-for-profit partners Selfhelp Realty Group and Riseboro Community Partnership Inc., were awarded the Sumner Houses site by the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) and New York City’s Department of Housing Preservation & Development (HPD) through an RFP process.

The result is the Atrium at Sumner, the new 11-story mixed-use senior building, designed to Passive House standards by world renowned Studio Libeskind Architects. The Atrium consists of 190 studio and one-bedroom apartments and the ground floor has an 8,000-sq. ft. program for all inclusive care for the elderly. The building is certified to Enterprise Green Communities and New York State Energy Research Development Authority (NYSERDA Tier II). The unit mix and affordability levels conform to HPD’s Senior Affordable Apartments Rental (SARA) program. 

The Development Team was awarded Project Based Section 8 vouchers for all apartments, which was underwritten at 110% of HUD Fair Market Rent. Thirty percent (30%) of the units will be set aside for formerly homeless individuals. Social Services will be provided to all residents through Selfhelp’s Housing with Services model, with comprehensive case management services provided to the formerly homeless residents. The community facility, PACE, will be operated by Riseboro and Elderserve.

Tours will be led by Matthew Gross, Owner and Builder at Urban Builders Collaborative LLC, Lettire Construction Corp.

sites.name: Bayside Historical Society Castle
sites.description:
Completed in 1887, The Castle at Fort Totten served as the Officers Mess Hall and Club for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers School of Application. Perhaps the greatest significance of The Castle is the direct architectural tribute it pays to the emblem of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, who centered most of their activities at Willets Point from 1866 to 1902.

The Castle in Fort Totten is one of the finest surviving examples in New York City of the Gothic Revival castellated style architecture. This architectural style was developed in Great Britain in the mid-1700s and brought to this country in the early 1800s. The popularity of the Gothic Revival style marked a turning away from earlier classical styles based on the building of ancient Greece and Rome. Gothic style features present in The Castle exteriors include octagonal crenelated corner towers, lower central gatehouse, and drip molds over the windows.

In 1982, when the Army considered relinquishing parts of Fort Totten, then-Senator Frank Padavan, a retired US Army Corps of Engineer Officer who had served as Chief of Staff at Fort Totten, assisted the Bayside Historical Society (BHS) in leasing and beginning restoration of the building in 1984. BHS has been caring for The Castle ever since. 

BHS docents will provide tours of The Castle that cover the history of the building and it's restoration, current use of the building, including a local archeology room, review of artifacts from the early 1900s, and more. Visitors will have access to the current exhibit,  "Home Front & Front Lines: 250 Years of American Service."
sites.short: Tour the historic 1887 Gothic Revival Castle in Fort Totten Park and learn about its unique architecture and restoration, featuring early 1900s artifacts and access to the "Home Front & Front Lines: 250 Years of American Service" exhibition.

sites.description:
Bella Abzug Park is a burgeoning linear park in Hudson Yards. Stretching from West 33rd Street to West 37th Street between 10th and 11th Avenues, the park was built in conjunction with the development of Hudson Yards. An engineering marvel, the park is partially built over the 7 train station and will eventually have two additional blocks built over Amtrak train tracks. The park features unique landscape elements throughout its four blocks, with each block tailored to its unique urban microclimate that results from the dynamic shade, sun, and wind from surrounding buildings. 

Join David Torres, Director of Field Operations, and Chris Gendron, Lead Horticulturalist, with the Hudson Yards Hell's Kitchen Alliance to learn about the conception of the park, its future, and the work it takes to maintain healthy plants and trees in a new and changing neighborhood.
sites.short: Learn about the innovative design and evolving landscape of a linear park built over active train lines, and get insider insights from the team behind its creation and ongoing care.

sites.name: Better Sheds Ahead
sites.partner: Practice for Architecture and Urbanism (PAU) and LERA Consulting Structural Engineers
sites.description:
Get a first look at the next generation of sheds, designed to fix what generations of New Yorkers have learned to tolerate.

Selected by the NYC Department of Buildings, these new designs replace the familiar flat deck and plywood parapet with a sloped roof that opens the sidewalk to the sky, discourages climbing, and sheds water more effectively, all while remaining code-compliant and budget-conscious through a standardized "kit of parts" that adapts to the city's wildly varied sidewalk widths, building heights, and densities.

Visitors will see full-scale mockups of the new shed system and learn how details most people walk past without a second thought, were reconsidered to improve circulation, safety, and daily life on the sidewalk below. Expect to hear about the removal of street-level bracing and corner columns that currently create pedestrian bottlenecks and vehicle hazards. 

Architects from PAU and structural engineers from LERA will host the tour together, offering participants a chance to engage directly with infrastructure that shapes everyday city life and to see how thoughtful design can transform even its most overlooked corners.
sites.short: Explore full-scale mockups of innovative sidewalk sheds featuring open-air designs while architects and engineers reveal how reimagined details enhance pedestrian flow and daily urban life.

sites.name: BioBAT at Brooklyn Army Terminal

address.note: Building A, Ground Floor Lobby.

sites.description:
Presented in celebration of Climate Week NYC 2026 and the launch of BATWorks—NYCEDC’s clean-tech and climate innovation hub at Brooklyn Army Terminal—the new exhibition "Living Matter, Shaping Futures" invites visitors to imagine material frontiers and multispecies perspectives that might redefine how we manufacture, design, and live.

As ecological pressures and shifting climate patterns compel us to reconsider the systems that shape human society, the exhibition illuminates the interdependence of living systems and offers a hopeful vision of the future—one grounded in resilience, reciprocity, and ecological intelligence. Here, critical technologies are understood not as separate from nature, but as embedded within the complex web of life.

The featured works expand the limits of human-centered design by recognizing cognition, agency, and creativity across nonhuman species, microbial networks, and technological ecologies. Together, they propose new ways of understanding intelligence—not as individual dominance, but as a capacity that emerges through collaboration, interrelation, adaptation, and responsiveness.

Echoing author James Bridle’s proposition that intelligence is distributed across planetary networks, "Living Matter, Shaping Futures" encourages visitors to listen more closely to forms of knowledge that exceed the human. The exhibition asks how art and design might help us cultivate more reciprocal relationships with the organisms, materials, infrastructures, and technologies that sustain our shared future.

Featuring Antía Iglesia Fernández, Danielle Parsons, Fiona Bell, Interspecies Library, Lolo Ostia, and Peter Yeadon. Curated by Elena Soterakis.
sites.short: Explore innovative artworks and technologies that challenge human-centered design by highlighting the intelligence and creativity found in nonhuman species, microbial networks, and ecological systems, inspiring new ways to live and collaborate with the natural world.

sites.name: Black Bedford-Stuyvesant Memories 1930's–1970's Walking Tour
sites.description:
The A and C trains brought thousands of Southern and Caribbean migrants to Bedford-Stuyvesant during the first and second waves of the Great Migration. Fulton Street remains the primary commercial artery today; however, the community has changed. Although the jazz venue sites have been demolished or repurposed, most of the businesses of that era are no longer on Fulton Street. This tour remembers the rich jazz, business, and civil rights legacies of the community as well as local trailblazers, businesses, and institutions such as the old Boys and Girls High Schools and Restoration Corporation.

On the tour, participants will walk through the streets that produced luminaries such as Max Roach, Randy Weston, Jitu Weusi, Judges John Phillips and William Thompson, Andrew and Jocelyn Cooper, Joan Maynard, Bertram Baker, Ernesta Procope, Bethann Hardison, June Jordan, Paule Marshall, Roxie Roker, Una Mulzac, Hattie Carthan, Elsie Richardson, Dr. Adelaide Sanford, Dr. Josephine English, and the women of the United Order of The Tents, to name a few, and the multitudes who labored in obscurity
sites.short: Explore the legacy of a historic Brooklyn neighborhood, walking the same streets as influential artists, activists, and community leaders while uncovering stories of both celebrated and unsung trailblazers.

sites.name: Bohemian National Hall
sites.partner: Bohemian Benevolent & Literary Association, Consulate General of the Czech Republic in New York, Czech Center New York, and Dvorak American Heritage Association
sites.description:
Built in 1896 and designed by architect William C. Frohne in the Renaissance Revival style, Bohemian National Hall is a rare surviving example of the social halls established by New York City’s immigrant communities in the nineteenth century. For more than a century, the building has been at the heart of Czech and Slovak life in New York. From its earliest days, it served as a gathering place for the community, offering Czech language and history classes, traditional food, cultural programs, celebrations, and spaces for social and civic life. Today, the Hall remains an important reminder of the vibrant immigrant community that once flourished in Yorkville and of the broader history of immigration in New York City.

In 2001, ownership of Bohemian National Hall was transferred from the Bohemian Benevolent & Literary Association (BBLA) to the Czech Republic. Following an extensive renovation, the building continues its original cultural mission and today is home to the Consulate General of the Czech Republic in New York, Czech Center New York, and BBLA, alongside other Czech organizations and initiatives.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors are invited to step inside this historic building, discover its architecture and interiors, and learn more about the organizations that keep it active today. The Dvořák Room will also be open to visitors. Dedicated to composer Antonín Dvořák and his years in New York, the room preserves the legacy of one of the most important connections between Czech and American musical history and is maintained by the Dvořák American Heritage Association.
sites.short: Step inside this historic building, explore its Renaissance Revival architecture, and learn about its enduring role in Czech and Slovak culture.

BookOps is a shared library technical services organization that serves the Brooklyn Public Library (BPL) and New York Public Library (NYPL) systems. BookOps is jointly governed and funded by NYPL and BPL and carries the responsibility of meeting the strategic collection management and distribution needs of each organization.

On this tour, participants will learn about how BookOps acquires, describes, prepares, and delivers new items for BPL and NYPL's circulating collections, and for the general collections of NYPL’s research libraries. Come see the largest public library book sorter in the country, that sorts and delivers close to 7 million books to public library branches in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan and Staten Island.

sites.name: Bowne House Historical Society
sites.description:
Bowne House (built circa 1661) is the oldest home in the borough of Queens and was occupied by members of the Bowne family for nearly 300 years. The remarkable history of the site includes family patriarch John Bowne’s defense of religious tolerance & liberty of conscience, as well as later family members’ participation in the 19th-century Abolition movement and a New York network of the Underground Railroad. 

OHNY Weekend visitors will be able to explore the garden and three period rooms while learning about the history of Bowne House and the neighborhood of Flushing, from past to present. The permanent collection on view includes historic furniture, collection artifacts, and copies of archival documents. 

Plus, enjoy a Pop-Up Exhibit of four recently conserved embroidered samplers from the Bowne House Collection! These delicate samplers are rare examples of early American needlecraft and will be temporarily on view for the Bowne House OHNY Weekend program.

Due to limited space inside the historic period rooms, visitors will be allowed staggered entry based on check-in time.
sites.short: Step inside a historic home to explore period-accurate rooms and gardens, view original artifacts and archival documents, and see a special pop-up exhibit of rare early American embroidered samplers on display for a limited time.
sites.access_notes:
Due to the historic structure of the home, wheelchair accessibility is limited. All open rooms are on the first floor of the house. Rooms are connected via short ramps and there is a portable ramp for entry into the front door, which is the only access point for entry. There are no ADA restrooms on site. For questions about accessibility, visitors are encouraged to email bownehouseeducation@gmail.com.

No food or drink allowed inside the museum. Please no pets, except for service animals. No photography inside the museum. Please leave large bags and backpacks in the entryway.

sites.name: Bronxlandia
sites.description:
A historic rail station is making new history for the South Bronx.

Although the years have not been kind to this 100+ year-old Cass Gilbert-designed structure, it endures in ruinous grace. It's an early American example of steel-reinforced concrete construction that served as a rail station for its first 27 years and then was subdivided into retail storefronts when rail service was shut down. 

Most recently, local resident, MacArthur Fellow, Peabody Award winner, author and Princeton University professor Majora Carter acquired the building from Amtrak and has set about working on its revitalization, now operating it as Bronxlandia, an exciting event venue.

A tour of the structure with a presentation of archival images and architect renderings for future renovations will be shared on OHNY Weekend. Those dressed for adventure can even climb a ladder up into the attic and down into the cellar.

Visitors are encouraged to check out the neighboring Boogie Down Grind Café at 868 Hunts Point Avenue to see photos, signage, and other artifacts from the area as well as the nightclub that occupied the building in the 1970s-80s.
sites.short: Visit a historic, century-old rail station with a guided tour featuring archival images, future renovation plans, and rare access to the attic and cellar, plus a chance to view local artifacts and memorabilia at a nearby café.

sites.description:
The Brooklyn Army Terminal is an architectural and engineering marvel that is today a center of manufacturing and innovation on Brooklyn’s Sunset Park waterfront. Built to supply American forces in World War I, this enormous Cass Gilbert-designed complex served as a supply base for the American military for nearly 50 years, employing more than 20,000 people during World War II. Today, this thriving industrial park is home to over 100 companies in a wide array of industries, from precision manufacturers to artists, online retailers to food manufacturers. 

During BAT’s open access hours, the Building B atrium along with several tenant sites will be open to OHNY Weekend visitors, including galleries and studios for Sunset Park Open Studios.

sites.name: Brooklyn Borough Hall
sites.description:
"…a dignified civic structure of impressive scale…"
— NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, 1966 designation decision

Brooklyn Borough Hall is Brooklyn's oldest public building, and now houses the offices of the Brooklyn Borough President. Originally built as Brooklyn's City Hall, it once contained the offices of the Mayor, the City Council, a courtroom, and a jail — typical of early nineteenth-century city halls that housed all functions of government under one roof.

Brooklyn was incorporated as a city in 1834, and a design competition the following year was won by architect Calvin Pollard. Financial troubles stalled construction after the 1836 cornerstone-laying; building resumed in 1845 with a simplified design by Gamaliel King, and the incomplete City Hall opened in 1848. It served as Brooklyn's City Hall for fifty years until the 1898 consolidation with New York City, when it became Brooklyn Borough Hall.

The Greek Revival structure is clad in Tuckahoe marble, with a monumental staircase leading to six fluted Ionic columns and a triangular pediment. Its cast-iron cupola is an 1898 replacement after an 1895 fire; the statue of Justice atop it, part of the original plan, wasn't installed until 1988. Architect Gamaliel King was a major figure in 19th-century Brooklyn architecture, also responsible for the now-demolished King's County Courthouse and the surviving King's County Savings Bank. The building's rotunda and 1903 Courtroom, designed by Axel Hedman, feature restored marble floors, coffered domed ceilings, and carved wood paneling.

A designated New York City, New York State, and National Register landmark, Brooklyn Borough Hall underwent an award-winning restoration in the 1980s that repaired its exterior stonework, cupola, and roof. During OHNY Weekend, visitors can see the restored rotunda and 1903 Courtroom up close, and learn about the building's nineteenth-century construction history, its architects, and the decades-long restoration that brought its exterior and interior details back to their original state.
sites.short: Step inside this landmark’s restored rotunda and 1903 Courtroom—normally closed to the public—to admire original marble floors, domed ceilings, and carved woodwork while discovering the building’s rich architectural history and award-winning restoration.

sites.name: Brooklyn Conservatory of Music
sites.description:
Since 1944, the Brooklyn Conservatory of Music (BKCM) has occupied one of Park Slope's most beautiful historic mansions, a five-story Victorian brownstone at the corner of 7th Avenue and Lincoln Place. This fall, the beloved non-profit community music school is expanding to a second, 12,000-square-foot location within One Prospect Park West, an equally storied 1925 Classical Revival building on Grand Army Plaza.

During OHNY Weekend, guests are invited to tour both of BKCM’s locations and learn about their history – and the unique design challenges that PBDW Architects and Consigli Construction addressed as they outfitted the lower level of a historic residential building to be a state-of-the-art facility for music education and music therapy, from sound treatment to accessibility. 

Tours are led by Miranda Knutson, BKCM's Senior Events and Community Partnerships Manager, and each will include a guest speaker to explore a distinct aspect of the Conservatory’s citywide work.

The 2 PM tour will focus on history and design, with special insights about our architectural needs.

The 3:30 PM tour invites guests to hear from staff at the new BKCM Music Therapy Institute, which will be housed in the One Prospect Park West space. 

The 5 PM tour will explore these buildings' pivotal role in BKCM's citywide music education and music therapy programs, which operate in 90 schools and community-based organizations across the five boroughs.
sites.short: Tour two architecturally significant music school spaces, gain behind-the-scenes insights into their historic renovations and design challenges, and hear from experts about the Conservatory’s citywide music education and therapy initiatives.
sites.access_notes:
Both of the Conservatory’s locations are wheelchair accessible. Guests can access Brooklyn Conservatory of Music Prospect Park West through a new, ADA-accessible ramp. All floors of the 58 Seventh Avenue building can be accessed by elevator.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Brooklyn Glass
sites.description:
Brooklyn Glass is a working glass studio where traditional glassblowing techniques meet contemporary art and design. Since opening its doors, the studio has served as a creative hub for artists, students, and the public, offering classes, workshops, studio rentals, and demonstrations in glassblowing, flameworking, and neon.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors will have the opportunity to step inside an active glass studio and observe the process of working with molten glass firsthand. Watch artists and instructors gather, heat, shape, and manipulate glass to transform a glowing mass of molten material into a finished object.

Brooklyn Glass is dedicated to making glassmaking accessible to a broad community, providing opportunities for both beginners and experienced artists to explore the medium. OHNY Weekend offers a chance to experience the studio as a working creative space and see the people, tools, and processes behind the finished work.
sites.short: Step inside an active glass studio to watch artists transform molten glass into finished pieces, with live demonstrations in glassblowing, flameworking, and neon.

Founded in 2010, locally based Brooklyn Grange is the leading rooftop farming and intensive green roofing business in the US, fostering more livable and climate-adapted cities by restoring the connection between people and the natural world through food, education, and events. This 3.2-acre rooftop farm and event space—Brooklyn Grange's largest—overlooks New York Harbor, downtown Manhattan, and Lady Liberty.

Visit Brooklyn Grange during Fall Fest and celebrate the end of the growing season. Tour the farm, learn how Brooklyn Grange feeds the surrounding community, and engage with community partners throughout the day.

sites.name: Brooklyn Navy Yard: Creative Currents
sites.description:
Explore cool spots, meet makers, and dive into history at the Brooklyn Navy Yard Annual Open House!

Discover the Yard’s 300-acre innovative campus during the Annual Open House, part of Open House New York Weekend. Step inside the studios of businesses in fashion, design, and technology for exclusive behind-the-scenes access and immersive activations. This day celebrates Brooklyn Navy Yard's campus of makers and offers artists, designers, entrepreneurs, and neighbors alike the chance to connect with peers, explore our campus and the businesses who thrive here, and experience the innovation at the Yard up close.

On your visit, follow the **Creative Currents** track with a color-coded map provided at check-in to explore Brooklyn Navy Yard as a home for art in all forms. 

Creativity flows through the Brooklyn Navy Yard; home to hundreds of artists, ranging from painters to photographers to jewelers. They'll be opening their studios to the public, inviting audiences in for an exclusive opportunity to view their work, learn about their processes, inspirations, and their journeys. Come take a rare behind-the-scenes look at the artistry that flourishes at the Yard, and leave feeling inspired.
sites.short: Visit the workspaces and design studios of dozens of artists working at the Brooklyn Navy Yard to see their processes, inspirations, and journeys.

sites.name: Brooklyn SolarWorks
sites.description:
Located in Gowanus, Brooklyn SolarWorks opens its rooftop to show what’s possible when solar meets city living. Designed specifically for New York’s ubiquitous flat-roof buildings, Brooklyn SolarWorks' solar canopy shows how renewable energy can fit seamlessly into dense urban neighborhoods while preserving usable outdoor space.

Visitors will step under an active solar installation and see firsthand how innovative design makes solar power possible in the five boroughs. The team will share how these systems are built, how they power homes, and why they are key to a sustainable future for NYC. Learn about the unique challenges of urban solar, from navigating historic buildings to maximizing limited roof space, and how thoughtful design overcomes them.

As a company rooted in New York City, Brooklyn SolarWorks is proud to open its doors and its rooftop space to share what they have built. Come experience a solar-powered space, enjoy views of Brooklyn, and discover how solar can transform the way New Yorkers live.
sites.short: Step under an active rooftop solar installation with sweeping views of Brooklyn and learn directly from experts about how innovative design makes solar power possible in the five boroughs.
sites.access_notes:
Access to the office requires climbing two flights of stairs, and the roof requires an additional flight of stairs.

Strollers are not allowed.

Visitors during OHNY Weekend will visit the historic Dime Savings Bank at the base of the tower and the 90th floor apartments that exhibit works from Stickymonger and Silver Art.

sites.name: Brotherhood Sister Sol
sites.description:
Discover the headquarters of The Brotherhood Sister Sol (BroSis), a nationally recognized Harlem-based youth development and social justice organization that has empowered Black and Latinx young people for more than 30 years. Opened in 2022, the building is one of the few purpose-built community education centers constructed in New York City in recent years—dedicated entirely to youth development, leadership training, community organizing, and social justice, without residential or commercial uses.

Designed by Minority- and Women-Owned Business Enterprise (MWBE) firm Urban Architectural Initiatives, the state-of-the-art facility reflects BroSis's mission through thoughtful architecture, sustainable design, and spaces created for learning, healing, recreation, and collective action. Visitors will explore gathering spaces, educational environments, and mission-driven design elements throughout the building, including its rooftop basketball court, a unique feature that underscores the organization's commitment to the holistic development and well-being of young people. Tours will highlight BroSis's history, its impact on Harlem and beyond, and how the building serves as a hub for youth leadership, policy advocacy, professional training, and community transformation.

Visitors will also have the opportunity to experience the adjacent Frank White Memorial Garden, a 6,000-square-foot Environmental Learning Center co-designed and built by BroSis youth members and local residents. The site features an urban farm producing more than 35 varieties of fruits and vegetables, a greenhouse, aquaponics system, challenge course, and community gathering spaces. Guests will learn how youth leadership, environmental stewardship, and community-driven design come together to create lasting change.
sites.short: Tour a state-of-the-art youth development center which cultivates leaders and builds community, featuring innovative learning and recreation spaces, a rooftop basketball court, and an urban farm.

sites.name: Caribbean Cultural Center African Diaspora Institute
sites.partner: Caribbean Cultural Center African Diaspora Institute (CCCADI)
sites.description:
The Caribbean Cultural Center African Diaspora Institute (CCCADI) invites you to experience "Jab, J’ouvert, Revelry and Resistance," a landmark exhibition marking our 50th anniversary. Curated by Know Your Caribbean, the exhibition immerses visitors in Carnival as a powerful living expression of resistance, identity, memory, and joy.

Rooted in Afro-Caribbean histories, "Jab, J’ouvert, Revelry and Resistance" traces Carnival’s transformation from acts of rebellion under oppression into vibrant traditions of freedom, creativity, and collective expression. Across generations and geographies, Carnival becomes both celebration and archive—a space where histories are remembered, identities affirmed, and communities come together.

Enter a multisensory world of sound, texture, archival materials, contemporary art, and interactive experiences. Moving through layered environments, visitors encounter Carnival not simply as a spectacle, but as an embodied language—one that lives in the movement of the body, the rhythms of memory, and the passage of time.

Part installation, part archive, and part altar, the exhibition reveals the cultural connections that bind the Caribbean Diaspora while honoring its rich diversity and complexity.

Presented as a cornerstone of CCCADI’s 50th anniversary celebration, Carrying a 50 Year Legacy of Justice, Joy and Resistance into the Future, the exhibition invites you to witness, feel, and celebrate Carnival as a living legacy.
sites.short: Be immersed in a multi-sensory exhibition exploring Carnival as a living legacy of resistance, identity, and joy, featuring interactive art, archival materials, and layered environments that reveal the cultural connections and vibrant traditions of the Caribbean Diaspora.

sites.name: Carnegie Hall
sites.description:
Take a guided tour and enjoy an insider’s look at the world-famous national landmark. Discover more than 130 years of Carnegie Hall and music history, including secrets about the Hall’s legendary acoustics and little-known stories about its iconic performances.

Walk through sections of the majestic Stern Auditorium / Perelman Stage, explore rare musical scores in the Composers Gallery, and view invaluable musical artifacts in the Rose Museum. Please note that due to the Hall’s busy performance schedule, tours do not include backstage or onstage access.

Guests will be divided into five equal-sized groups prior to the start of the tour. Participants are asked to remain flexible and stay with their Docent once assigned to keep everyone who arrives in one party together.
sites.short: Be immersed in over 130 years of music history, uncovering the secrets of legendary acoustics, rare musical scores, and unique artifacts, while touring exclusive areas like the Stern Auditorium and Composers Gallery.

sites.description:
Tucked away on the sixth floor of The General Society of Mechanics and Tradesmen, the Institute of Classical Architecture & Art's Cast Hall displays a collection of historical plaster casts of Classical and Renaissance architecture and sculpture alongside fragments of historical woodwork from significant buildings and country houses in the United Kingdom.

The Cast Hall at the Institute of Classical Architecture & Art is a gem of 19th-century New York City's art collecting past. Filled with plaster casts originally owned by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, the gallery now plays host to scores of visitors, ranging from students to practicing artists. Visit the Cast Hall for open sketching and to learn about this historic art practice and collection.
sites.short: Explore a hidden gallery filled with rare plaster casts of Classical and Renaissance art and enjoy open sketching sessions in this historic space that was once part of New York’s 19th-century art scene.

sites.name: Castle Williams
sites.description: Castle Williams is a circular defensive work of red sandstone on the northwest point of Governors Island in New York Harbor. It was designed and erected between 1807 and 1811. Designed by the Chief Engineer of the US Army Corps of Engineers, Lt. Col. Jonathan Williams, for whom the fort is named, it is considered a prototype for the next generation of coastal fortification. It is one of the earliest examples of a Casement-style fort and a key aspect of the harbor defense system of New York Harbor in the early decades of the 19th century. The tour will be led by a National Park Service Ranger.
sites.short: Tour a pioneering 19th-century circular fortification with a National Park Service Ranger and learn about its unique casement-style design and role in early harbor defense.

address.note: Entrance for Synod Hall is at the south end of the St. John the Divine Campus.

sites.description:
Explore Synod Hall, a rarely accessible building on the campus of the world-famous Cathedral of St. John the Divine. This wonderful example of neo-Gothic architecture was built in 1913 by the architectural firm Cram & Ferguson to host councils and conventions of church officials. Synod Hall was built to reflect the Cathedral's art and architecture, with its carved timber roof beams and colorful grisaille windows adding more intimate details. The facade of Synod Hall is the most concentrated on the Cathedral campus, with dozens of individual carvings all telling important stories.

Enjoy this exclusive OHNY Weekend access by exploring at your own pace, with Cathedral staff available for periodic brief "Tour Talks."

The Cathedral grounds are open on the weekends. After visiting Synod Hall, participants are encouraged to explore the Cathedral's gardens and grounds.
sites.short: Explore the Cathedral of St. John the Divine's Synod Hall during OHNY Weekend. Built in 1913, this neo-Gothic masterpiece features detailed carvings, timber roofs, and staff-led talks.

sites.partner: Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine
sites.description: Since 1981, a lesser-known program of the Cathedral has been the Textile Conservation Lab, or TCL. Tucked away on the Close in what was an 1830’s orphanage, the TCL cares for St. John the Divine’s historically significant 17th-century English and Italian tapestry sets. Over the years, textile conservators have slowly and carefully cleaned, conserved, and remounted half of the treasured collection while also taking on textile conservation projects from all over the country, from high-profile museums to locals who may own a special quilt or sampler. Go behind the scenes with textile conservators Marlene Eidelheit and Valerie Soll to see up close what types of varied textile projects the Textile Lab is working on these days and hear about the process.
sites.short: Hear from expert textile conservators and witness the meticulous restoration of centuries-old tapestries to discover how the lab preserves historic textiles from both major museums and private collections.

sites.description:
As the flagship public architecture school in NYC, The Bernard and Anne Spitzer School of Architecture at the City College of New York is committed to shaping the future of the built environment. For OHNY Weekend, visitors are invited to a rare, behind-the-scenes look at where tomorrow's designers and urban thinkers hone their craft.

Visitors will explore a variety of unique academic and creative spaces on a drop-in basis. Step into a cutting-edge Robotics Lab to see how advanced technology is transforming architectural fabrication, and visit the Sorkin Reading Room, dedicated to its namesake, Michael Sorkin, a distinguished late professor of architecture. Take in the sights from the newly renovated rooftop, a spectacular vantage point. 

In the exhibition gallery, visitors will discover "Design Matters: In Favor of Urban Public Space." This timely exhibition celebrates the 25th anniversary of the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona (CCCB) European Prize for Urban Public Space, offering profound insights into the design and preservation of shared urban environments.

Make a day of it: the historic Great Hall of Shepard Hall at CCNHY is also open for Drop-In visits on Saturday.

Built from the Manhattan schist bedrock on which they perch, its buildings feature a rich array of delightful terra cotta grotesques reflecting the academic disciplines originally housed within.

sites.description:
The Center for Brooklyn History (CBH) at the Brooklyn Public Library is home to the largest collection of Brooklyn-related materials in the world. CBH's ever-expanding collection includes more than 1,600 archival collections, 300,000 photographs, 300 paintings, and 8,000 artifacts. For OHNY Weekend, CBH will provide exclusive access to highlights from these collections by offering a tour of the onsite storage of art, artifacts, and archival holdings in the collections, typically closed to the public.

The Center for Brooklyn History will also be offering a building tour, offering an insider perspective to the 1881 landmark building, as well as curator insight into the exhibitions currently on display. The building dates back to an 1879 architectural contest for the best design for a building to serve the Long Island Historical Society (CBH's original name). Designed by George Post, the highly recognizable terra cotta brick exterior, mesmerizing stained-glass windows, and two-story reading room make the building a standout in Brooklyn and in the city at large. Come experience the building, inside and out, from the perspective of CBH's insiders!
sites.short: Get rare behind-the-scenes access to the Center’s vast art, artifact, and archival collections, usually closed to the public on guided tours of the landmark 1881 building with curator insights into current exhibitions and striking architectural features.

sites.name: Central Park's Grand Army Plaza South

address.note: Meet at the corner of West 59th Street and Fifth Avenue.

sites.description:
Join Central Park Conservancy guides for an in-depth look at Grand Army Plaza, one of the Park’s historic entrances. In June 2026, the Conservancy completed a $16 million restoration of Grand Army Plaza South and reopened the space to the public.

As part of the restoration, the Conservancy’s team carefully balanced historic preservation with modern infrastructure and accessibility upgrades to the space: detailed conservation of the Pulitzer Fountain’s Pomona statue, replaced bluestone paving and granite curbs, new pedestrian lighting, and landscape restoration and plantings to reflect the historic design.  

Redesigned in 1916, the plaza’s grand design inspired by Place de La Concorde in Paris, was a departure from Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux’s original vision that rejected park entrances marked by monuments. Incorporating two symmetrically designed islands separated by 59th Street, the reimagined south entrance embraced monumentality, featuring the towering monument to Union Army General William Tecumseh Sherman in the north plaza and the Roman Goddess of plenty, Pomona, standing atop the Pulitzer Fountain in the South Plaza.   

Conservancy guides will lead short drop-in tours and answer questions about restoration details, sharing insights that typically lay unseen and are sure to inspire. You can expect to connect the history of Grand Army Plaza (and why there’s another in Brooklyn!) to the designs of celebrated artists who—in their contributions to the Park—go on to inform one of the most profound experiences in nature anywhere in the world.
sites.short: Explore the newly restored gateway to Central Park with expert guides, featuring behind-the-scenes insights into historic preservation, modern upgrades, and the stories behind its iconic monuments and design.

sites.description:
Central Synagogue is a stunning Moorish Revival architectural landmark in Midtown Manhattan. Enter the sanctuary to learn about its architecture, the history of the synagogue's community, and experience the stories of New York City Judaism past, present, and future.

Docents will provide mini-tours throughout the sanctuary space. Visitors will have an à la carte opportunity to jump on as many mini-tours as they want, as well as visit the lower level exhibition space. The synagogue's current exhibition features a didactic journey through provenance research, bringing to life the stories of paintings, furniture, books, and other objects that were taken from Jewish families during WWII.

For security reasons, all visitors must complete a registration form for entry. Registration will be available on-site but advance registration is recommended: <https://events.blackthorn.io/f44KAiM7/5a46PfB4v6D>

Photography and video is permitted, but please ask your docent for permission before filming. They have the right to refuse.

sites.partner: NYC Department of Records & Information Services (DORIS) and Citygroup Inc.
sites.description:
Discover the layers of change sustained by the historical buildings that make up some of New York City's oldest surviving urban fabric on this walking tour through the Lower East Side. Led by architect-researcher team Violette de la Selle and Wes Hiatt, participants will visit some fascinating buildings that exemplify dominant building types in the area (loft building, school, tenement, and residential hotel), peeling back layers to understand how much the buildings have transformed and evolved since their initial construction.

The tour concludes at the NYC Department of Records and Information Services, with a first look at the duo's upcoming exhibition, Changing Change, featuring drawings, photographs, and revealing records from the Municipal Archives and Library that piece together these unexpected, composite histories.
sites.short: Trace the evolution of iconic Lower East Side buildings with architect-researcher guides and enjoy exclusive early access to an upcoming exhibition that reveals hidden stories behind the neighborhood’s historic architecture.

websites.title: NYC Department of Records & Information Services

sites.access_notes:
The walking tour will take place on NYC streets and cover approximately 1.34 miles. Participants can expect to encounter narrow spaces, uneven terrain, and several large street crossings. Comfortable, closed-toe shoes are recommended.

The final stop, 31 Chambers Street, requires a brief security screening, including a magnetometer and bag check, to enter. It is an accessible building with an ADA entrance located at street level on Reade Street (rear of the building). Elevators are available on all public floors. If you have specific accessibility needs or questions, please contact publicprograms@records.nyc.gov in advance. 

The tour is recommended for ages 16+. Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Church of the Transfiguration
sites.partner: Church of the Transfiguration, Episcopal Actors' Guild, and Houghton Hall Arts Community
sites.description:
Join the Church of the Transfiguration for a full weekend of music, art, and history celebrating its long tradition of diversity and inclusion! Since it was built in 1848, the historic Church of the Transfiguration (Episcopal) has provided a beautiful, safe, welcoming space to visitors from all denominations and from around the world. This year marks 177 years of diversity and inclusion… from serving as a stop on the Underground Railroad to being the first NYC church to do funerals for actors.

Come hear these and other stories from “The Little Church Around the Corner" during OHNY Weekend tours. Hear wonderful musical performances on a Fiske organ or the Bosendorfer piano (including a family-oriented concert). Enjoy the historic archives of the Episcopal Actors' Guild, which has supported the arts and artists in New York City for a century. Learn about church textiles, enjoy the art gallery, and more!
sites.short: Experience a weekend of music, art, and history with guided tours, live performances on historic instruments, access to rarely seen archives of the Episcopal Actors' Guild, and insights into the church’s unique legacy of diversity and inclusion.

The Church is wheelchair-accessible, including bathrooms. Most areas are accessible by mobility scooter.

Brochures are available in multiple languages, and a Spanish-language tour will be offered. 

Service and emotional support dogs are allowed on leashes. 

Flash photography is not permitted during performances.

If any children have taken a serious interest in singing, the children’s choirs offer excellent musical education and many performance opportunities. Information on auditions will be available after the concert on the organ platform.
sites.special:
**Saturday Activities:**
- **10:30 AM–3 PM Church Vestments Exhibit**. Vestments are more than just beautiful robes worn by clergy! The colors, patterns, and fabrics all come together to tell a story. Many new and antique vestments will be on display, and former fashion industry professional Steve Leavitt will be on hand to share information and answer questions. Steve is the owner of Transfiguration Vestments, a Manhattan shop that makes, repairs, and restores vestments, altar covers, and other church textiles. 
- **10:30 AM–3 PM Theatre Archives Exhibit. **The Episcopal Actors’ Guild invites visitors to take a peek inside their archives featuring memorabilia from George Holland, Joseph Jefferson, and Edwin Booth, and other famous actors associated with the Church of the Transfiguration. In front of the Edwin Booth window in the transept.
- **10:45 AM History Tour** celebrating the Church’s 178 years of diversity and inclusion. Hear about the Underground Railroad, the Draft Riots of the Civil War, the “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot” stained glass window, the church’s special relationship with the theatre community, and more. Learn how Transfiguration came to be the church that has married more couples than any other church in America (including the first gay marriage in the Episcopal Church). Meet the tour guide in the chapel near the entrance.
- **1:15 PM Theatrical Tour** by Eric Stamm, Archives chair of the Episcopal Actors Guild. Learn about the Church's history through a theatrical lens. View stained glass windows and plaques of actors and hear stories of how the Episcopal Actors' Guild and "The Little Church Around the Corner" have opened their doors to the theatre community (and everyone else) throughout its history. Meet the tour guide in the chapel near the entrance.
- **3 PM** **Piano Concert** by world-renowned artist Matei Varga, playing the Church's sumptuous Bösendorfer grand piano (once owned by William F. Buckley!). He will perform several classical works and share his insights on the various pieces. Don’t miss this opportunity to see a former child prodigy, now a world-class musician, playing beloved pieces on a prized instrument. 

**Sunday Activities:**
- **12:30 PM Guided Tour in Spanish/Visita guiada en español **celebrando los 178 años de diversidad e inclusión de la Iglesia.

The Church of the Village is home to the United Methodist faith community and is a progressive, LGBTQ+ affirming church with a long history of allyship and advocacy with the queer community. Located directly across from The Center (The Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Community Center), the building was the site of the very first PFLAG Meeting (formerly called Parents, Families, and Friends of Lesbians and Gays). Inside, visitors will find stunning stained-glass windows, high ceilings, beautiful chandeliers, and more. 

During OHNY Weekend, Church of the Village will offer tours of its space, sharing the history of LGBTQ+ advocacy in the building and community, while offering its signature hospitality to the community.

sites.name: City Reliquary Museum
sites.description:
The City Reliquary is a portal to a version of New York City that spans all of its memorable eras. Like a cabinet of curiosities on a large scale, the museum is a beautifully arranged collection of rare and humble artifacts from all five boroughs. Subway tokens and World's Fair souvenirs share space with remnants of landmark buildings and beloved local businesses, each one with a unique story. A site "off the beaten path" in bustling Williamsburg, the City Reliquary is truly one of New York City's best-kept secrets. 

Explore a brand-new exhibition about Manic Panic, the NYC-based hair dye and cosmetics brand founded by sisters Tish and Snooky Bellomo, that added color to the goth and punk scene in NYC in the early 1980s.
sites.short: Browse quirky artifacts from every era of NYC history, including rare subway tokens and local memorabilia, and catch a new exhibition on Manic Panic, the iconic brand that brought bold color to the city's punk and goth scenes.

sites.description:
Special for OHNY Weekend, Community Carbonates is coming to the Climate Imaginarium to demonstrate their innovative way to capture CO₂ through engineered flowstones, a nature-inspired, distributive technology. Built on existing infrastructure and designed for indoor use in buildings, flowstones transform ambient CO₂ into mineral carbonates used as construction materials. Beyond carbon capture, the flowstone also improves air quality, reduces energy usage, and boosts productivity, making it a meaningful climate solution within reach of everyday communities. Community Carbonates is an initiative of the Global Impact Lab at the Columbia Climate School.

The Climate Imaginarium will also host New School Prof. Kathleen Sweeney’s presentation of a special sneak peak into the design process of EcoAction cards game which was sponsored by Cornell Cooperative Extension Climate Futures project.

A select panel of exhibiting artists will also be present throughout the weekend to introduce their role in the “Witness to Change” climate data Climate Imaginarium main exhibition.

The Climate Imaginarium is a center for climate, community, and culture in New York City. Located on Governors Island, the Climate Imaginarium is activating a cultural destination at the heart of New York City’s burgeoning green economy, where artists, scientists, advocates, and storytellers come together to reimagine and build a more resilient future.
sites.short: Experience live demonstrations of an innovative CO₂-capturing process, get an exclusive preview of the EcoAction cards game design process, and meet artists behind the “Witness to Change” climate data exhibition.

Visitors can also explore the museum's exhibits and participate in hands-on activities at the imagiNATIONS Activity Center and Sit and Sew program.
