sites.name: Colossal Media Paint Shop
sites.description:
Picture an auto shop that moonlights as a paint store, art studio, and painted signage museum. That's the home of Colossal Media, the global leader in hand-painted outdoor advertising.

Founded and based in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, Colossal adds murals to meaningful places for authentic engagement to communities around the world. The hand-paint craft is a careful process that engages passersby and is an inherently tactile and highly skilled art form. It transforms any ad into a performance, an experience, and a reveal. Every mural Colossal paints begins in its Los Angeles or Brooklyn paint shop, with a meticulous pre-production system.

Visit Colossal's Brooklyn warehouse to learn about how it has been custom-outfitted for large-scale mural production. 

Check out "We Paint" — a Colossal Media short film dedicated to walldogs. Before digital billboards, there were walldogs—skilled artists who scaled buildings to paint advertisements by hand. ‘We Paint’ documents the high-stakes, high-impact world of modern large-scale mural painting, honoring the legacy of these unsung artists. Watch here: https://youtu.be/Fu7sYfO3uBI
sites.short: Explore the artistry behind large-scale hand-painted murals at a working warehouse where skilled painters create meaningful places for authentic engagement in communities around the world.

Located at the edge of the East Village in Manhattan, the design and appearance of the facility is very much driven by the adage "form follows function." The various functions of the facility—making electricity, generating high pressure steam, safely and reliably serving customers—dictate the configuration and design of the station.

sites.description:
Go behind the scenes at Cornell Tech and explore three programs within the Tata Innovation Center: the Game Assemblies Lab, the MakerLAB, and Cornell University's College of Architecture, Art, and Planning (AAP) NYC Center. Visitors will discover how students, researchers, artists, and designers use these spaces to prototype ideas and address real-world challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration.

Join Niti Parikh, founding director of Cornell Tech's MakerLAB, for a tour of the space, which combines digital fabrication, hands-on making, and collaborative learning to help students, researchers, and community partners turn ideas into physical prototypes. Parikh will share how the MakerLAB grew into a 2,700-square-foot learning and research environment, and how initiatives such as CRAFT @ Large and Make:Health connect Cornell Tech with communities across New York City.

Directed by architect, game designer, and associate professor José Sánchez, the Game Assemblies Lab will highlight video game research projects in development, exploring collective coordination and how design emerges through game systems and digital platforms. Visitors can test interactive prototypes and talk with researchers about each project's goals.

Guided by Executive Director Robert W. Balder, explore the Cornell University College of Architecture, Art, and Planning (AAP) NYC Center, a 13,000-square-foot studio, exhibition, and event space located on the fourth floor of Cornell Tech's Tata Innovation Center. The center serves students studying architecture, urban design, city and regional planning, and design technology. Visitors will tour the flexible studio environment, learn about AAP's urban tech programming, and view student work from recent semesters.
sites.short: Explore three unique programs within a leading graduate campus and research center, including cutting-edge labs and studios where participants can test interactive game prototypes, and a state-of-the-art maker space with hands-on demonstrations.

sites.name: Custom Choking Signs as Folk Art, Science, and Visual Culture
sites.description:
Ever notice a choking poster in an NYC restaurant that looks suspiciously more like artwork than required safety signage? Maybe the post-apocalyptic one where the Heimlich participants are characters from the movie Escape from New York, or the Knicks-themed one where Spike Lee saves a choking Reggie Miller! On this unique walking tour, participants will visit four Williamsburg food service establishments to explore these custom choking-hazard signs as “cultural fingerprints,” instances of folk art, science communication, and visual design unique to NYC. 

Tours will be led by Rhea Kapur, a researcher, engineer, and archivist who studies computer science and linguistics at Stanford and photographs choking posters to better understand real-world communication. To what extent do custom graphics and punchy text turn them into creative artworks rather than ordinary signs? How does that work within the constraints of the law? Oral histories Rhea has collected from illustrators and restaurateurs reveal that the signs emerged in the mid-2010s (alongside the rise of social media and branding), in a city with an astonishing density of restaurants whose service industry survives off its abundance of creatives.

This tour shares both sides, discussing the linguistic and graphical intricacies of choking posters and their stories. Participants will see each poster within the context of each restaurant’s design: how do they fit the color scheme? Are they framed? Why? This tour invites participants to eschew NYC’s fine-art gallery scene and to consider art, science, and design innovation everywhere around the city.
sites.short: Explore four Williamsburg establishments to discover quirky, custom choking-hazard posters and learn how these creative signs blend art, science, and design, guided by an expert who shares insider stories from illustrators and restaurateurs.

address.note: Enter the Derfner Judaica Museum at the Jacob Reingold Pavilion Circle, inside Hebrew Home at Riverdale Main Campus.

sites.description:
"Taking a Broad View: Portrait Photography from the Collection" features more than two dozen images from the Derfner Judaica Museum + Art Collection by fourteen photographers working in the United States from the late nineteenth through the early twenty-first centuries. The photographers featured employ a variety of portrait genres, including traditional headshots, candid portraits, environmental portraits, and group and family portraits. Their subjects reflect a range of American identities, from Frédéric Brenner's women rabbis, cantors, faculty, and students in Manhattan to Larry Fink's young girl preparing for her first communion in the Bronx, from GisMo's Cuban American princesses in Miami to Toba Tucker's Pueblo community members in the Southwest, and such icons of celebrity culture as Ray Charles, James Dean, Betty Friedan, and Pete Seeger, among others.

The exhibition, marking the 250th anniversary of the United States, considers the role photography has played in constructing social identities, especially when the camera is wielded by outsiders to the communities represented, as well as the opportunities for self-reflection when photographers turn the camera on themselves. It also demonstrates how photographers establish empathy with their subjects, modeling and expanding that empathy to viewers.
sites.short: Explore a diverse collection of American portrait photography spanning over a century, featuring rarely seen images that highlight varied identities and communities, with a special curator-led tour offering unique insights into the art and its social impact.

sites.partner: NYC Department of Sanitation and Dattner Architects
sites.description:
This tour offers a behind-the-scenes look at Brooklyn Community District Garage 3, a 220,000-square-foot Department of Sanitation facility that redefines what civic infrastructure can be. Located in Bedford-Stuyvesant, the building houses 68 sanitation vehicles and supports the daily work of approximately 120 DSNY employees, while presenting a thoughtful and welcoming presence within a predominantly residential neighborhood.

Designed by Dattner Architects, the award-winning project reflects the firm's long-standing commitment to essential architecture: public buildings that perform complex operational functions while contributing positively to the civic realm. The facility's facades combine expansive areas of glass with faceted precast concrete panels, creating a dynamic architectural expression that communicates transparency, durability, and civic pride. Above, a 46,000-square-foot green roof and photovoltaic canopy help advance the City's sustainability goals, demonstrating how critical infrastructure can support environmental performance as well as operational efficiency.

During the tour led by Paul Bauer, Partner, and Patrick McAffrey, Associate Principal at Dattner, visitors will learn about the architectural and urban design strategies that shaped the project, including its relationship to the surrounding neighborhood, sustainability features, material palette, and public-facing design elements. Participants will also gain insights into the day-to-day operations of the facility and the critical role it plays for the neighborhood. Discussions will explore how vehicles, personnel, equipment, and building systems are organized to support 24-hour operations, as well as how the design balances security, functionality, staff well-being, and community engagement.
sites.short: Step inside a state-of-the-art sanitation facility to explore innovative architecture, sustainability features like a green roof and solar canopy, and how the design supports 24/7 operations, staff well-being, and community engagement.

Visitors will also get a close-up look at the Department’s Class 8 Vehicle Emissions Testing Laboratory, a state-of-the-art innovation center and one of only a few such facilities in the country.

Every winter, DSNY removes snow and ice from the approximately 19,000 lane-miles of City streets and organizes snow removal from public areas like bus stops, crosswalks and fire hydrants and step streets. Learn about the technology the Department uses during the winter season, and tour the renowned Spring Street Salt Shed, designed by Dattner Architects.

sites.name: DSNY Staten Island Compost Facility
sites.description:
DSNY's Staten Island Compost Facility is the largest such facility in the city. Food scraps and yard waste are turned into finished compost on the site, located by the old Fresh Kills landfill. The facility has produced about 42 million pounds of finished compost per year over the last several years. The site also accepts food scraps and yard waste from NYC agencies and nonprofits, yard waste from commercial landscapers, and hosts seasonal compost giveback events. 

Recently, the DSNY celebrated a major expansion of capacity at the Compost Facility that includes new equipment—known as an aerated static pile—that increases the facility’s capacity to turn food waste into compost by nearly 2,000%. 

Tour the facility with DSNY and learn about its high-tech operations.
sites.short: Tour the city's largest compost facility, explore cutting-edge technology that boosts composting capacity by 2,000%, and see how food scraps and yard waste are transformed into valuable compost.

sites.name: Edge NYC
sites.description:
Perched 100 stories above Hudson Yards, Edge NYC offers a rare opportunity to experience New York City from within one of its most distinctive contemporary architectural landmarks. Extending nearly 80 feet out from 30 Hudson Yards, the outdoor sky deck appears to float in midair, supported by a complex structural system engineered to create unobstructed views across the city.

During this special OHNY Weekend experience, visitors will explore the design and evolution of Edge NYC, from its new immersive indoor environments developed by globally recognized design firms to its dramatic outdoor sky deck—the highest in the Western Hemisphere. Guests will discover how architecture, engineering, digital media, lighting, sound, and interactive art work together to shape the journey through the space.

The tour will highlight Edge’s newly reimagined indoor experience, including installations that transform familiar views of New York through light, sound, and reflection, and build anticipation for the ascent to Level 100. Visitors will also learn about the creative and technical collaboration required to operate an immersive attraction within a working skyscraper, as well as the behind-the-scenes considerations involved in producing events and experiences more than 1,100 feet above Manhattan.

Hudson Yards Experiences operates Edge and brings together architects, artists, designers, engineers, hospitality teams, and creative partners to continually reimagine how visitors encounter New York City. OHNY Weekend guests will leave with a deeper understanding of the design decisions, technology, and daily operations behind one of the city’s most recognizable destinations.
sites.short: Ascend to a world-famous sky deck, exploring newly reimagined immersive indoor installations and learning how architecture, engineering, and interactive art combine to create a unique experience over 1,100 feet above Manhattan.

sites.name: FABSCRAP Warehouse at Brooklyn Army Terminal
sites.description:
Ever wondered what happens to unused fabric, samples, and design scraps from the fashion, interior design, and entertainment industries? Step inside FABSCRAP’s warehouse to find out.

On this behind-the-scenes guided tour led by Julie Mastrarrigo, Business Operations Consultant, you’ll learn how FABSCRAP has worked with more than 900 brands and thousands of volunteers to divert pre-consumer textile waste from landfills through reuse, recycling, and community action. Participants will discover the scale of pre-consumer textile waste, observe material processing and collection, and get a crash-course in FABSCRAP's material sorting processes while exploring the re-use room. Whether participants are designers, sustainability enthusiasts, students, or simply curious, this is a chance to “Follow the Fabric” and see textile reuse and recycling solutions in action.

Beyond material diversion, FABSCRAP has cultivated one of the nation's most engaged local textile reuse communities. Through volunteer programs, educational initiatives, public access to recovered materials, and industry partnerships, the organization empowers individuals and businesses alike to participate in circular systems!
sites.short: See how pre-consumer textile waste is sorted, processed, and given new life through exclusive access to material reuse operations and insights into large-scale recycling efforts usually unseen by the public.
sites.access_notes: Children 12+ welcome. Every person attending, including children, must have a ticket.

On these special tours during OHNY Weekend, visitors will go behind the scenes to see production and distribution spaces and learn how this massive former military complex has been adaptively reused for modern industry. Each tour will visit multiple spaces on a different theme.

**Made at BAT: 11:30 AM **- Get a rare inside look at some small- and medium-sized manufacturers to see the wide diversity of products and production taking place inside the Brooklyn Army Terminal.

**Circular Economy & Sustainability Tour: 2:30 PM** - The Brooklyn Army Terminal has also developed a cluster of companies committed to sustainability, working in fields ranging from energy efficiency to upcycling to waste reduction.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes to see production and distribution spaces and learn how a massive former military complex has been adaptively reused for modern industry.

sites.name: Federal Hall National Memorial
sites.description: Federal Hall National Memorial marks the site where George Washington was inaugurated as the first President of the United States. It is also the site where the First Congress met. The original Federal-style building was torn down in 1812. The current hall, a Greek Revival building intended for use as a custom house, was built between 1834 and 1842 by the architects Alexander Jackson Davis and Ithel Townes. In 1862, it became a subtreasury bank, and then served as the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1920 to 1924.
sites.short: Step inside the monument that marks the historic site where George Washington took the oath of office and the First Congress convened, a striking Greek Revival building that has served as a custom house, subtreasury, and Federal Reserve Bank.
sites.access_notes:

This tour explores the history of environmental degradation in Gowanus and the emerging movement for housing and environmental justice along the canal, a movement led by local organizers with the Gowanus Neighborhood Coalition for Justice (GNCJ) who fought to ensure an equitable rezoning of the neighborhood in 2021.
 
Walking tours will be led by Fifth Avenue Committee's Executive Director Michelle de la Uz.
sites.short: Join a guided walking tour led by a local organizer to explore Gowanus’ environmental history, the fight for housing and environmental justice, and the community-led efforts behind the neighborhood’s equitable rezoning.

sites.name: Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church
sites.description: Step inside one of New York’s last remaining Gilded Age treasures. Completed in 1875, the church predates the nearby St. Patrick’s Cathedral (1878) and Plaza Hotel (1907). The stunning ceiling of this Victorian Gothic masterwork rises six stories above the floor. The 1,800-seat Sanctuary contains no iconography (in keeping with early Presbyterian austerity) and no right angles; the curvature of the balcony and pews draws all eyes to the impressive pulpit.
sites.short: Visit a Gilded Age landmark featuring a soaring six-story Victorian Gothic ceiling and an 1,800-seat sanctuary with unique curved architecture.

sites.name: Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church Organ Tour
sites.description: Renowned musician Dr. Patrick Kreeger, Fifth Avenue Presbyterian’s associate organist, will lead a special demonstration of the Sanctuary organ, affectionately known as the “Mighty Austin.” Built in 1961 by the Austin Organ Company of Hartford, Connecticut, the organ has four keyboards, a pedalboard, and 119 ranks. Patrick begins with a history of the organ, which contains parts dating back to 1855. His demonstration highlights the many colors and sounds that are found within the chambers of this 7,500-pipe instrument.
sites.short: Experience a rare, up-close demonstration of the “Mighty Austin” organ, as a renowned musician shares its fascinating history and showcases the diverse sounds of this 7,500-pipe masterpiece, including parts dating back to 1855.

sites.name: Flatiron Building at Dusk
sites.partner: Beyer Blinder Belle Architects & Planners and L'Observatoire International
sites.description:
The Flatiron Building is an instantly recognizable icon of New York City. Designed by Daniel Burnham and constructed in 1902 by the Fuller Company as one of the first steel-framed skyscrapers in New York, it became famous through the then-novel medium of photography, which highlighted its dramatic prow—the result of its triangular site at the intersection of Broadway and Fifth Avenue—and Beaux-Arts ornamentation. Today it is undergoing conversion into 38 luxury condominium residences by the Brodsky Organization, with exterior restoration by Beyer Blinder Belle and exterior facade illumination by L’Observatoire International.

This tour is led by Carlos J. Cardoso, Partner, and Pooya Amin-Javaheri, Associate, from Beyer Blinder Belle, and Benjamin Légier, Communications Director, and We Jien, Project Director, from L'Observatoire International. Participants will circumnavigate the perimeter of the Flatiron Building at dusk as the tour highlights the history of the building, the restoration of the ornate limestone and terracotta facade, the reconstruction of historic elements like the revolving door at Fifth Avenue and 22nd Street, the discovery of a lost balcony at the prow of the building, and—once night falls—the dramatic LED illumination that gives it an all-new presence in the skyline.
sites.short: Explore a NYC icon's storied past and recent restoration on a perimeter walking tour highlighting its ornate facade, reconstructed historic details, and a striking LED light display that transforms its nighttime appearance.
sites.access_notes:
This tour will take place entirely outdoors; there is no access to the interior of the Flatiron Building. Participants will be standing throughout. Dress for the weather and wear comfortable shoes.

The nearest restroom is in Madison Square Park.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Floyd Bennett Field Bike Tour
sites.partner: Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy and National Park Service
sites.description:
Join Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy for a unique biking tour through the past, present, and future of New York City’s first municipal airport—now part of Gateway National Recreation Area and one of the city’s most extraordinary natural and historic landscapes. This guided ride will take you across some of Floyd Bennett Field’s vast runways and hidden trails, highlighting its aviation history, important natural areas that provide critical habitat for birds and other wildlife, ongoing restoration efforts, and the careful stewardship that helps protect this special place. The bike tour will be led by JBRPC Executive Director Terri Carta and Communications Coordinator Sean Lenehan.

The tour begins in front of the Ryan Visitor Center, where participants will be introduced to Floyd Bennett Field before proceeding to historic Hangars 3 and 4 to learn about the exciting plans for their adaptive reuse. These landmarked buildings are poised to be transformed into a dynamic destination for community and art events, food and beverage offerings, visitor amenities for adventures in nature, and a new hub for nature-based jobs and technologies. 

Cycling the original concrete runways, the ride will head through the North 40 Natural Area, Jean Bourque Memorial Bird Blind overlooking a freshwater pond, Raptor Point and the Seaplane Ramp, and the Marian Heiskell Native Grass Nursery, Ecology Village, and the Floyd Bennett Field Archery Range. The final stop of the tour will be at the fishing beach on Rockaway Inlet – the gateway to Jamaica Bay, one of the most ecologically significant estuaries in the region – before heading back to the Ryan Visitor Center.

Tour Details: Approximately 6 miles, flat terrain on paved and packed surfaces. Suitable for beginner cyclists; ages 12 and up. Participants should bring their own bicycles, helmets (mandatory for all riders), and water.
sites.short: Pedal across historic runways and hidden trails on a guided bike tour exploring aviation landmarks, rare wildlife habitats, and behind-the-scenes restoration projects.
sites.access_notes:

The bike journey is suitable for beginner cyclists: approximately 6 miles of flat terrain on paved surfaces. The group will dismount bikes and walk around at various points of the tour to explore natural spaces and Hangar B. 

Access to the tower at the Ryan Visitor Center requires the use of stairs. There is no elevator available.

There are limited food options nearby, so participants are encouraged to bring snacks to the bike ride. Much of the ride will be on open runways with limited shade; riders should wear sun protection.

sites.name: Floyd Bennett Field Ryan Visitor Center & Hangar B
sites.partner: Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy and National Park Service

address.note: Enter via Ryan Visitor Center.

sites.description:
Experience the Golden Age of Aviation at Floyd Bennett Field! Now part of the National Park Service's Gateway National Recreation Area, Floyd Bennett Field served as New York City's first municipal airport beginning in 1931, quickly becoming the country's most technically sophisticated airport. The Ryan Visitor Center, formerly the administration building and glamorous terminal for the airport, has been restored by the National Park Service. The terminal was a modern marvel of its time, where well-heeled travelers enjoyed amenities including a restaurant, barbershop, and newsstand, as well as a cocktail bar with views looking out over the airport's runways. The terminal now houses a museum telling the story of Floyd Bennett Field and the famous aviators who flew there, Amelia Earhart and Howard Hughes among them. 

During OHNY Weekend, visitors may tour the museum and take a peek at the tunnels underneath the runways, not generally open to the public, where airport staff transported travelers' luggage to their planes. Visitors can also enter the restored control tower, also not generally open to the public, offering panoramic views of Jamaica Bay and the airport's runways and grasslands. It's one of the best views in Brooklyn! Rangers will also be available at Hangar B, on the shores of Jamaica Bay, approximately one mile east of the Ryan Visitor Center. Home of Floyd Bennett Field's Historic Aircraft Restoration Project (HARP), Hangar B contains dozens of restored and model aircraft, including a full-scale model of Wiley Post's Lockheed Vega, the "Winnie Mae,” in which he became the first aviator to fly solo around the world.
sites.short: Tour the restored 1930s airport terminal and museum, explore rarely accessible underground luggage tunnels and the control tower with sweeping views, and see dozens of historic aircraft—including a full-scale model of the "Winnie Mae"—at the working restoration hangar.
sites.access_notes:
Access to the tower and tunnel require the use of stairs. No elevator is available. 

Hangar B is approximately 0.75 miles east of Flatbush Avenue by car, bike, or on foot.

sites.name: Ford Foundation Center for Social Justice
sites.description:
The Ford Foundation building was commissioned by Henry Ford II in the 1960s. The architectural firm of Kevin Roche John Dinkeloo and Associates designed a soaring, inspiring space for the foundation’s headquarters: a radically transparent building of glass, granite, and Corten steel, occupying a near-perfect square that stretches the width of the block between 42nd and 43rd streets. The 12-story enclosed atrium garden, designed by Dan Kiley, was the first of its kind in the United States.

The historic atrium garden and Ford Foundation Gallery will be open to OHNY Weekend guests. The 11th Floor Overlook and the Ford Family Auditorium, not typically open to the public, will be available to view as well. Guided tours will be led by Ford Foundation staff members Faith Lim, Hospitality Services Coordinator; Roy Pacheco, Lobby Ambassador; and Anthony Sims, Facilities Associate.

Note: not all ticketed tour slots are the same.
11 AM, 1 PM, and 3 PM sessions are guided tours.
10 AM, 12 PM, and 2 PM sessions are self-guided experiences.

No large photography equipment, tripods, or flash photography is permitted.

sites.name: Frick Collection
sites.description:
As part of OHNY Weekend, The Frick Collection is offering free admission on Friday, October 16, from 9:30 AM to 12:30 PM.

The Frick is New York City's home for art from the Renaissance to the late nineteenth century, displayed in one of New York City’s last great Gilded Age mansions. Open since 1935, the museum offers intimate encounters with one of the world’s foremost collections of European fine and decorative arts—including celebrated works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Fragonard, Turner, and more. 

During OHNY Weekend, learn how the Frick mansion became The Frick Collection with a signature gallery talk, _A Home for Art. _Visitors are also invited to explore the Frick Art Research Library. Discover the beautiful reading room, including a brief talk on the historic space’s architecture. Throughout the event, a mobile book cart featuring selections on architecture from the library will be available in the museum’s Elizabeth M. and Jean-Marie R. Eveillard Hall.

Also on view: Siena: The Art of Bronze, 1450–1500: the first exhibition to focus on Siena as a center of artistic excellence and technical innovation in bronze sculpture during the Italian Renaissance. Bringing together some forty works—most of which have never been exhibited outside of Tuscany—the exhibition invites visitors to appreciate the medium’s beauty and versatility while learning about the complex technical and political challenges that the Sienese bronzeworkers faced.

Round out your day with a stop at the Museum Shop for all your Frick-inspired gifts, plus grab a refreshing beverage or pastry at our coffee bar or dine at our full-service café, Westmoreland.
sites.short: Enjoy free morning admission to view masterpieces by Vermeer, Rembrandt, and more in a historic mansion, plus exclusive access to rare Sienese Renaissance bronzes never before shown outside Tuscany.

The Frick Collection encourages visitors to utilize available accessibilty resources. For more information, visit frick.org/accessibility.

During the OHNY Weekend Drop-In hours on Friday, October 16, walk-up visitors are welcome. Free timed tickets are also available for those who wish to reserve in advance.

Visitors must be 10+.

sites.name: From Roots to Arts at Astoria Houses
sites.partner: Public Housing Community Fund, The Urban Conga, and Tamra Cosby
sites.description:
At Astoria Houses, public art becomes a platform for community voice, memory, and connection.

Visitors will experience Revolving Voices, an interactive public sculpture created by local artist Tamra Cosby in collaboration with The Urban Conga and Astoria Houses residents through From Roots to Arts, an artist-in-residence program bringing arts and cultural investment to NYCHA communities across New York City.

Rather than bringing a finished artwork into the community, Revolving Voices was shaped through months of community engagement sessions. Poetry, spoken word, storytelling, and community conversations informed its design, expanding the possibilities of what public sculpture can represent and whose voices are preserved in public space.

During the tour, visitors will explore the sculpture and learn how residents, artists, community organizations, and City partners collaborated to transform a shared space at Astoria Houses. The tour will also explore poetry and spoken word as forms of fine art alongside sculpture and design.

Through From Roots to Arts, the Public Housing Community Fund works alongside NYCHA, artists, community partners, and residents to ensure public housing communities have a meaningful role in shaping the art within their neighborhoods. Revolving Voices demonstrates what is possible when community is the foundation and legacy is the objective. The tour will be led by Kemi Karim, Senior Manager of Art & Culture at the Public Housing Community Fund, with Tamra Cosby and The Uran Conga co-founders Ryan Swanson and Maeghann Coleman.
sites.short: Experience an interactive public sculpture shaped by community voices, where poetry, spoken word, and storytelling inform both the art and its meaning, and discover how residents and artists collaborated to transform a shared space through creative engagement.

sites.name: From Roots to Arts at Bronx River Houses
sites.partner: Public Housing Community Fund, Bronx River Houses Resident Association, Tats Cru, and Mark Lawrence
sites.description:
At Bronx River Houses, public art becomes a living archive of history, memory, and cultural legacy.

On this OHNY Weekend tour, participants will experience two resident-centered public artworks created through From Roots to Arts, an artist-in-residence program bringing sustained arts and cultural investment to NYCHA communities across New York City. Inside the Bronx River Community Center, visitors will explore a permanent photo mural created in partnership with Photoville and shaped by an extensive community archival process. More than 300 photographs were collected and scanned from residents, preserving decades of everyday life, celebrations, relationships, and memories at Bronx River Houses. The installation transforms a shared community space into an archive where residents can see themselves and their history permanently represented.

The tour will also visit The Home That Inspired the World, a large-scale outdoor mural celebrating Bronx River Houses’ 75-year history and its connection to the cultural legacy of hip-hop. Developed with artist Mark Lawrence, TATS CRU, and residents, the mural honors the people, stories, and creative traditions that have shaped the community. Visitors will learn how archival preservation, community engagement, and public art can work together to tell a fuller story of public housing beyond its architecture. The tour will be led by Kemi Karim, Senior Manager of Art & Culture at the Public Housing Community Fund, and Norma Thomas, Tenant Association President at Bronx River Houses, with artist Mark Lawrence.
sites.short: Discover a photo archive and resident-driven mural that celebrate decades of community life and hip-hop heritage, offering insight into the lived experiences and cultural legacy of the residential community celebrating its 75th year.

sites.name: FUJIKINA NYC 2026: Scavenger Hunt Photowalks
sites.description:
**Booking this experience is a two-step process**. Review the "Policies" section below for full details.

Like Open House New York, FUJIKINA NYC 2026 opens doors—literally and conceptually—to the stories that make our city extraordinary. The festival celebrates the 200th anniversary of photography with guided photowalks that reveal the rich visual and architectural character of the Lower East Side through the eyes of master photographers.

Why the Lower East Side? This historic neighborhood tells stories of immigration, resilience, and creative culture through its layers of tenement architecture, fire escapes, and densely woven urban spaces. It’s long been a pilgrimage site for photographers documenting American life. The neighborhood’s tight streets and varied facades offer endless visual possibilities and architectural richness that rewards careful observation.

During OHNY Weekend, join a scavenger hunt photowalk led by accomplished photographers Hayden Goldsworthy and Chris Berry. Participants will learn how photographers see and frame the built environment, noticing light, composition, and the human stories embedded in architecture. The walk teaches visual literacy—how to spot moments and meaning in everyday urban spaces—and reveals the Lower East Side’s soul and creative potential. It’s suited to anyone interested in photography, history, or how architecture shapes community.
sites.short: Join a small-group photowalk and scavenger hunt led by expert photographers, exploring the Lower East Side’s unique architecture and hidden stories while learning to see and capture the city’s visual and cultural richness via hands-on guidance.
sites.access_notes:
**Booking this experience is a two-step process.** An OHNY ticket alone does not guarantee admission. OHNY ticket holders will receive a code to book a complimentary event ticket via Fujikina's website. 

Please bring a camera (and lenses) of your choice as this is a photography scavenger hunt. We'll be taking images on a guided walk for one hour around the Lower East Side.  

Participants are welcome to use the services at the Brand House before and after the walk.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Garry Grant Studio
sites.description:
Step inside the home and studio of New York–based artist Garry Grant for an intimate introduction to his life, work, and creative environment.

Grant has spent more than three decades developing a distinctive practice rooted in abstraction, African heritage, ancestral memory, and the recovery of histories that have been overlooked or forgotten. Working primarily with canvas, handmade paper, wood, mixed media, pigments, gilding, and found wood materials, he combines contemporary abstraction with traditional craft techniques to create richly layered works that explore identity, history, displacement, and cultural memory.

The visit offers guests a behind-the-scenes look at Grant’s working studio and an opportunity to experience his artwork in the environment where it is conceived, constructed, and developed. Visitors will see completed works alongside works in progress and learn about his materials, techniques, and artistic process.

The tour will also include a brief look inside Grant’s multi-story Harlem townhouse, which he and his family have restored and transformed over the years. Drawing upon his experience as a master gilder and professional frame restorer, Grant has personally incorporated restoration and design craft into the preservation and character of the home.

This OHNY Weekend visit offers a rare glimpse into the intersection of art, craftsmanship, home, and preservation—and into the personal space where an artist lives, works, and builds his creative practice.
sites.short: Visit an artist’s private studio and restored home, exploring his creative process, unique materials, and richly layered works that blend abstraction, African heritage, and traditional craft.
sites.access_notes:
Photos are permitted in the studio only. Guests must follow the instructions of the tour guides.

Visitors must be 18+.

sites.name: General Grant National Memorial
sites.description: Since 1959, the National Park Service has been the steward and caretaker of the final resting place of Ulysses S. Grant, the Commanding General of the United States (Union) Army during the American Civil War and later as the 18th President of the United States during Reconstruction. General Grant National Memorial is a tribute to the man who is credited with winning the Civil War, and is considered to be a symbol of gratitude from a thankful nation. Visitors to the memorial can expect to learn about the life of General Ulysses S. Grant, his contribution to the war, his goals and accomplishments as President, and will see these aspects of his life symbolized through Greco–Roman architecture.
sites.short: Explore the legacy of the 18th U.S. President through engaging exhibits and striking Greco–Roman architecture, highlighting Grant's pivotal role in the Civil War and his presidency during Reconstruction.
sites.access_notes:
The mausoleum is not an accessible building. There are no ramps or elevators leading to the entrance, and about 25 stairs lead to the entrance without handrails. 

The visitor center building is an accessible building and is located to the west of the mausoleum across the south bound lane of Riverside Drive.

sites.partner: The General Society and Institute of Classical art and Architecture (ICAA)
sites.description: The second-oldest library in the city includes a light-filled atrium that is used as a vibrant programming space by the General Society and other non-profits. Overlooking the Library on a striking wrought iron balcony is the John M. Mossman Lock Collection, which contains more than 370 locks, keys, and tools dating from 2000 BC to the early 20th century. The Society's archives and history date back to 1785. In addition to the Library and Lock Collection, the Society's distinctive Member's Assembly Room is also open to the public only on OHNY Weekend.
sites.short: Step inside a historic library in Midtown Manhattan, featuring a sunlit atrium for community events, a unique balcony display of over 370 ancient locks and keys, and rare public access to the Member's Assembly Room.

sites.name: gmp Architekten New York Studio
sites.description:
From the high-tech transformation of Real Madrid’s Estadio Santiago Bernabéu to mass-timber concert halls and low-carbon skyscrapers worldwide, discover the architectural concepts shaping our cities at the new Lower Manhattan studio of gmp · Architects von Gerkan, Marg and Partner.

Overlooking New York Harbor and the Statue of Liberty, the workspace opens for OHNY Weekend with a dynamic multimedia exhibition featuring architectural models, large-scale photography, and film. Meet the gmp team for direct insights into structural innovation, circular design, and Umbau—the practice of continuously converting and adapting existing structures to preserve resources and reduce embodied carbon.

Featured projects include Madrid’s modernized Bernabéu Stadium with its retractable roof, the revitalization of Munich’s massive Gasteig cultural center, and landmark civic infrastructure around the globe. This special studio visit will be hosted by Rosalind Tsang, New York Studio Director, Kristina Loock, Head of Business Development, and Tobias Keyl, Associate Partner.
sites.short: See cutting-edge architecture in a new way with a multimedia exhibition of global projects, access to architectural models and films, and direct conversations with the team behind sustainable design and innovative urban transformation.
sites.access_notes:
Visitors must pass through building security before entering. Please arrive on time, as the group will be escorted to the gmp studio together. Tickets are not transferable and latecomers may not be accommodated.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

Join the Gowanus Dredgers for a self-guided canoe tour of a fast-changing neighborhood. Launch from the Dredgers' custom community-built dock and explore the canal's history as an active industrial waterway through its ongoing transformation into a residential neighborhood. Guided audio tours developed by the Unheard-of Ensemble will be available, but are not required.

sites.name: Grand Central Terminal
sites.description:
A Beaux-Arts icon that first opened in 1913, Grand Central Terminal is one of New York City’s most heavily trafficked public spaces. In the 1970s, its significant use and fading luster fueled speculation about demolition; today, the terminal still stands, thanks in part to a high-profile preservation campaign led by former First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and architect Philip Johnson. 

Since 1990, Beyer Blinder Belle has worked on the revitalization of Grand Central Terminal, ensuring that America’s busiest train station continues to serve as a contemporary, multi-use transit and retail hub. This legacy has provided the BBB project team with unique insight into the terminal's iconic stories, unknown histories, and most recent evolutions.

Join Nathaniel Rogers, Principal, and Angela Curmi, Associate, of Beyer Blinder Belle Architects & Planners, for an in-depth tour of the public spaces at the Grand Central Terminal.
sites.short: Explore the Beaux-Arts icon's storied architecture and hidden histories on an in-depth tour led by the architects behind its revitalization, offering insider perspectives into America's busiest train station.

sites.name: Great Performances
sites.description:
Take an exclusive behind-the-scenes tour of New York’s premier catering and food service company, Great Performances, to see how this shop elevates life’s celebrations with vibrant flavors, gracious service, and unmatched professionalism.

Founded with a passion for the arts and a commitment to excellence, Great Performances has grown into a culinary powerhouse, operating numerous beloved restaurants, cafés, and concessions across the city, such as Dizzy’s Club, The Norm at Brooklyn Museum, and The Garden Court Café at The Asia Society. During OHNY Weekend, visitors are invited to explore the inner workings of the operation.

Join De'Enna Quinn, Inside Sales Associate, Molly Legrow, Senior Sales Administrator, and Carina Hayek, Director of Marketing, of Great Performances for this tour of the company's cutting-edge Bronx facility. Beginning in the first-floor commissary, follow the journey of ingredients from the moment they arrive at the loading dock, through various stages of preparation in walk-in refrigerators, cold kitchens, hot kitchens, and blast chillers. Tours will also visit the Sylvia Center, where Great Performances offers youth education about healthy eating; the Design and Marketing offices, where creativity comes to life; and the Design Warehouse—a veritable cave of wonders filled with everything needed to transform any event into a spectacular celebration.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes of a premier NYC caterer to follow ingredients from delivery to finished dishes, explore kitchens and creative offices to gain rare insight into how top-tier events are brought to life.

sites.name: Green-House at Green-Wood Cemetery
sites.description:
The Green-House at Green-Wood is the Cemetery’s new front door. Set around the restored 1895 Weir Greenhouse, this new space invites you to learn about Green-Wood before crossing onto the landscape itself. Green-Wood's restoration of the Weir Greenhouse was completed at the beginning of 2026, reopened to the public in April of 2026, and has already welcomed almost 20,000 visitors.

Founded in 1838 and now a National Historic Landmark, Green-Wood was one of the first rural cemeteries in America. By the early 1860s, it had earned an international reputation for its magnificent beauty and became the prestigious place to be buried, attracting 500,000 visitors a year, second only to Niagara Falls as the nation’s greatest tourist attraction. Crowds flocked there to enjoy family outings, carriage rides, and sculpture viewing in the finest of first generation American landscapes. Green-Wood’s popularity helped inspire the creation of public parks, including New York City’s Central and Prospect Parks.

Green-Wood is made up of 478 spectacular acres of hills, valleys, glacial ponds, and paths, throughout which exists one of the largest outdoor collections of nineteenth- and twentieth-century statuary and mausoleums. Four seasons of beauty from century-and-a-half-old trees offer a peaceful oasis to visitors, as well as its 580,000 permanent residents, including Leonard Bernstein, Boss Tweed, Charles Ebbets, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Louis Comfort Tiffany, Horace Greeley, Civil War generals, baseball legends, politicians, artists, entertainers, and inventors.
sites.short: Explore a beautifully restored 1895 greenhouse and discover fascinating stories of notable figures through artifacts from an extensive archive, or visit the studio of Green-Wood's artist-in-residence.
sites.access_notes: The Green-House at Green-Wood is a fully ADA accessible venue; however, once a visitor enters the grounds of The Green-Wood Cemetery, some spaces require stairs, steep inclines, and uneven terrain.

Additionally, Stephen Cassell, Principal at Architecture Research Office (ARO), will be showcasing his firm's work at the new Green-House at Green-Wood, an education and welcome center that wraps around the carefully restored Victorian-era Weir Greenhouse.

sites.partner: Brooklyn Greenway Initiative and Nelson Byrd Woltz Landscape Architects
sites.description:
Brooklyn Greenway Initiative built and maintains the Greenway Botanical Garden at the Naval Cemetery Landscape on the site of the former Naval Hospital Cemetery at the Brooklyn Navy Yard as a place for retreat and remembrance while honoring its rich layers of natural and cultural history. The Naval Cemetery Landscape is a native plant meadow and pollinator habitat, and provides visitors with an escape from urban life.

When visiting the Garden, visitors can also pick up a self-guided tour brochure at the entrance to learn more about the native meadow, the history of the Garden, and the site’s features. Gardeners will be on-site to dig deeper into our horticultural practices and to share nature observations. October is a great time to spot migratory birds, fall-blooming perennial plants, and various pollinators.
sites.short: Stroll through a native plant meadow and pollinator habitat, with a chance to hear from the landscape architect, or take a self-guided tour to learn about the history and ecology of the site.

There are no restrooms on site. 

Sun protection and mosquito repellent are recommended.  As a cemetery and wildlife habitat, dogs are not allowed on site. No bikes or scooters are allowed inside. A bike rack is available outside of the entrance. Nature photography only; all other photography requires a permit.

sites.name: Greenwich House Pottery
sites.description:
“Greenwich House Pottery is a New York treasure; alive, essential, awaiting your discovery. Greenwich House Pottery is one of the great gifts of New York.” —Jerry Saltz

Discover Greenwich House Pottery during OHNY Weekend with a behind-the-scenes visit to its Chelsea studio, where New Yorkers come together to learn, experiment, and create with clay.

Founded in 1909 as a workforce program for newly arrived immigrants, Greenwich House Pottery is one of New York City’s oldest ceramics communities. The Chelsea studio expanded the Pottery’s footprint beyond its historic Greenwich Village home, creating additional space for ceramics education and making.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors can explore the studio, see pottery wheel and handbuilding demonstrations, and get a closer look at the tools, materials, and techniques used by ceramic artists. Visitors can also experience the making process firsthand by contributing to collaborative community vessels or trying the pottery wheel during guided sessions for ages 8 and up.

From first-timers to experienced ceramicists, the OHNY Weekend offers an inside look at how a working pottery studio operates and how Greenwich House Pottery continues a more than century-long tradition of making, teaching, and supporting ceramic arts in the city.
sites.short: Visit a working pottery studio with guided demonstrations, hands-on opportunities to try the wheel or contribute to community vessels, and an inside look at the tools and techniques used by ceramic artists.

The entrance is ADA accessible and includes elevator access. The tour space is wheelchair accessible. An accessible pottery hand-building table is available; there is no accessible pottery wheel station.

sites.description: Trace the history and form of New York City's row houses in the early and middle decades of the 19th century. Representative houses and streets in Greenwich Village will demonstrate how these houses shaped New York's urbanism and development. The tour is led by Patrick W. Ciccone, preservationist and co-author of the revised Bricks and Brownstone, the classic history of the New York row house.
sites.short: Trace the evolution of 19th-century row houses and their impact on New York's urban landscape, guided by a leading preservationist and expert on historic architecture.

sites.name: Hall of Records Tour
sites.partner: NYC Department of Records & Information Services
sites.description:
Go back in time with the NYC Department of Records and Information Services' (DORIS) exclusive tour of the Surrogate’s Courthouse (originally known as the Hall of Records). Located in Lower Manhattan, this Beaux-Arts historical landmark is an example of the early 20th-century architectural movement, City Beautiful. Designed by John Rochester Thomas and completed in 1907 by Tammany Hall architects Horgan and Slattery, the building aimed to visually transform NYC, uplift the city’s communities, and inspire moral and civic virtue.  

The guided tour led by the Municipal Archives Digitization Specialist Matthew Minor takes participants through the building’s magnificent lobby and shares historical insights on the Palais Garnier-inspired grand staircase, mosaic ceilings, and interior sculptures.
sites.short: Explore an architectural gem with ornate interiors on a guided tour of a Beaux-Arts landmark, featuring  insights into the building’s rich history.

sites.name: Harborview Terrace
sites.partner: New York City Housing Authority, Public Housing Community Fund, and Grain Collective
sites.description:
At NYCHA’s Harborview Terrace Houses in Hell’s Kitchen, more than 33,000 square feet of open space has been transformed into a new commons: a network of places for play, gathering, gardening, recreation, and wellness. Developed through a resident-led process, the project brings together the Harborview Terrace Houses Resident Association, NYCHA, the Public Housing Community Fund, The Pershing Square Foundation, and Grain Collective to demonstrate how investment in public housing can strengthen both the physical and social fabric of a community.  

The tour will explore the recently completed second phase of improvements, including a new 14,000-square-foot intergenerational plaza with water play, planting, seating, and a large pyramidal climbing structure; a renovated outdoor fitness area; improvements to an existing community plaza and garden; and a revitalized recreation space serving older adults. Together, these spaces create opportunities for residents of all ages to gather, move, play, and connect.  

A central focus will be the participatory design process that shaped the project. Residents helped identify priorities and envision how their shared outdoor spaces could better serve everyday community life. The tour will also trace the development’s earlier improvements, including a 2023 sports zone with basketball and pickleball courts, murals, seating, planting, lighting, and accessibility upgrades, as well as new murals by artist Laura Alvarez.  

Participants will hear how landscape architecture, public art, philanthropy, and resident leadership came together to transform underused spaces into a new community commons.
sites.short: Tour newly transformed outdoor spaces featuring an intergenerational plaza, fitness and recreation areas, and vibrant murals—created through a resident-led design process that reimagined public housing for all ages.

sites.name: Harlem Grown
sites.description:
Experience Harlem Grown through the eyes of its Founder and CEO, Tony Hillery, on a special tour that brings the organization’s story, farm, and impact to life.

What began 15 years ago with Tony volunteering at a local Harlem elementary school has grown into a network of urban farms and programs centered on youth development, food justice, and community. During this special tour, Tony will share the story of how Harlem Grown began, including the moment neighborhood youth helped transform an abandoned lot into a thriving farm, and how that experience shaped the organization’s belief that when youth are given the opportunity to take ownership, they can transform their communities.

Visitors will explore one of Harlem Grown’s urban farm sites, including its farm, greenhouse, and mushroom chamber, and see firsthand how urban space can be used for growing, learning, and community connection. Tony will share stories from Harlem Grown’s 15-year journey and discuss how the organization uses urban agriculture to teach youth about healthy eating, sustainability, and where food comes from.

More than a farm tour, this is an opportunity to experience Harlem Grown’s philosophy firsthand: the organization grows more than food; it grows youth, families, and community.
sites.short: Join a founder-led tour of an urban farm, greenhouse, and mushroom chamber to hear firsthand stories of youth-led transformation and discover how urban agriculture empowers young people and strengthens community.

sites.partner: New York State Parks, Harlem River Coalition, Bronx and Harlem Rivers Urban Waters Federal Partnership, NY-NJ Harbor & Estuary Program, and Wilderness Inquiry

address.note: Head to the picnic tables for free canoeing and additional programming.

sites.description:
Canoemobile returns to Roberto Clemente State Park for the fifteenth year of the Harlem River Celebration on October 17th. Each year, the Celebration invites community members to visit the state park for a day of free public canoeing at one of the few publicly accessible launch sites on the Harlem River. The Celebration also features multiple educational, environmental, and arts tabling activities from community organizations and local, state, and federal agencies. 

The event is part of a larger program with Wilderness Inquiry, where hundreds of 5th and 6th grade students are brought to the Harlem River waterfront to participate in canoeing and tabling activities. The program is a collaboration with Wilderness Inquiry, Harlem River Coalition, Bronx Council for Environmental Quality, Bronx and Harlem Rivers Urban Waters Federal Partnership, NY-NJ Harbor and Estuary Program, and New York State Parks.

sites.name: Harlem River Houses Public Art Tour
sites.partner: ArtBridge, Settlement Housing Fund, NYCHA, and Mellon Foundation
sites.description:
Explore the intersection of public art, preservation, and community at Harlem River Houses, one of New York City’s most historically significant public housing developments. Opened in 1937, the nine-acre, 576-unit NYCHA complex was conceived as a model for affordable housing and incorporated significant public art and landscape features created through the New Deal’s Federal Art Project. 

Today, a new generation of site-specific artwork carries that legacy forward. Over the past year, NYC nonprofit ArtBridge led the installation of four permanent murals and four sculptures that speak to the cultural legacy of the Harlem River Houses community. Artists Paul Deo and Marthalicia Matarrita each painted two murals, while artist Kim Dacres created four sculptures. All artworks were designed through depthful consultation with Harlem River residents. 

Attendees will go on a walking tour of the public art installations, led by artists Paul Deo and Marthalicia Matarrita (both of whom are Harlem residents), with Harlem River Houses residents contributing their own insights about their community. 

As part of the event, attendees will engage in a Q&A with the artists, residents, and ArtBridge to discuss how contemporary public art can honor a landmark’s history and what’s needed to ensure that the voices and experiences of current residents become part of its evolving cultural legacy.
sites.short: Join a guided walking tour of newly installed murals and sculptures created in collaboration with Harlem River Houses residents, led by the artists themselves, and take part in a Q&A exploring how public art honors and evolves the community’s cultural legacy.

sites.name: Harlem River Walking Tour

address.note: Meet in the middle of The High Bridge.

sites.description:
Join NYC H2O for a two-hour walk along the historic waterfront of the Harlem River in the Bronx. This tour will visit several recently restored parks and landmarks on the Bronx coastline of the river, including the High Bridge, Highbridge Park and Step Street, and Bridge Park. It will end in Roberto Clemente State Park, at the annual Harlem River Celebration. Along the way, participants will hear about the forgotten history and ecologies of this remote shoreline, which was once home to wetlands, amusement parks, and steamship excursions. The tour will also consider the lack of public access on the Harlem River – along its entire shoreline in the Bronx, there are just two official access points to the water.

This walk will be led by Nathan Kensinger and Duane Bailey-Castro, who have been photographing the Harlem River for the past 15 years, and will include a look at their photographic work. This walk is part of a series called Walking the Harlem River, created for NYC H2O, a non-profit focused on water ecology in New York, and is generously supported by the New York-New Jersey Harbor & Estuary Program and the Hudson River Foundation. 

This walk is open to the first 40 drop-in attendees and is a one-way walk, starting at noon on the High Bridge and ending at 2 PM at Roberto Clemente State Park, as part of the annual Harlem River Celebration.
sites.short: Discover forgotten histories and ecologies on an adventurous walk exploring restored parks and hidden landmarks along the Bronx’s Harlem River waterfront.
sites.access_notes:
This is an outdoor walking tour covering 2.5 miles, and participants should dress for the weather and bring a water bottle. The route includes a long staircase and some uneven city streets, but is otherwise routed on paved sidewalks and pathways.

No dogs or pets permitted.

sites.name: Heliocentric Studios
sites.description:
Heliocentric Studio offers a rare opportunity to step inside a creative sound studio where architecture, acoustics, and music production converge. Designed by thread collective in collaboration with music producer Arun Pandian and acoustic specialist Ross Alexander, the studio reimagines the recording environment as an immersive, highly crafted space supporting both technical precision and material exploration. Every element, from material selection and lighting to spatial organization and detailing, has been shaped through the lens of acoustical performance to create an atmosphere that inspires focused listening, joyful experimentation, and playful collaboration.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors will enjoy a behind-the-scenes look at a professional recording studio typically reserved for private clients and small events. Guests will discover how architecture shapes the creative process, influencing the way music is recorded, mixed, and experienced. The studio balances sophisticated acoustic performance with a warm, tactile character. thread collective and Pandian found common ground in their admiration for Frank Lloyd Wright: thread through its restoration of the Olfelt Residence, and Pandian through Wright's design of the Rudy Van Gelder Studio. Painted red concrete floors, knotty wood ceilings, and soft uplighting reflect these influences.

thread collective will share the story behind Heliocentric Studio, highlighting the collaborative integration of architecture, sound, and technology. The project transformed a two-story brick warehouse through adaptive reuse and deep restoration, rebuilding it with thick insulated walls and triple-pane windows to isolate sound while insulating against the elements. A solar canopy, electrified building systems, heat recovery ventilation, and a native-planted green roof position the studio to meet Passive House standards while pairing technical excellence with environmental resilience.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes at a state-of-the-art recording studio, where innovative architecture, acoustics, and sustainability come together in a space designed for creative collaboration and technical excellence.

The tours will be led by an International Hildreth Meière Association Board Member and one of Hildreth Meière’s great-granddaughters.

sites.name: Hindu Temple Society of North America
sites.partner: The Hindu Temple Society of North America
sites.description:
The Hindu Temple Society of North America was incorporated on January 26, 1970, and completed the construction of the first Hindu Temple in North America in July 1977. Composed largely of imported granite and constructed by artisans from India, it is one of the most impressive and historically important Hindu Temples in the West. The temple has five large and four small black granite stone shrines with stone icons, 20 wall shrines with metal icons, five domes (four on all the cardinal directions and one 50-foot-tall tower facing east), a sunlit, glass-roofed walkway flanked by 16 granite stone pillars, artistically carved teak doors, and two pure silver chariots. View and learn about temple architecture, an array of divinities, and the rituals and services seeking blessings of knowledge, wisdom, wealth and prosperity, and protection. Be sure to stop by the Temple Canteen to purchase a delicious hot vegetarian meal!

This year, OHNY Weekend coincides with a Hindu Festival event, "Navaratri" or "Dussehra." This festival is observed for ten days between Sunday, October 11 and Tuesday, October 20. The theme of this festival is to honor all nine different forms of the Divine Feminine energy over nine nights, representing the inner spiritual journey of overcoming the darker qualities of the human mind.  Visitors will experience and enjoy the festivities, an added feature in 2026.
sites.short: Explore intricate temple architecture and sacred shrines, with a unique opportunity to experience a colorful festival honoring the Divine Feminine.

websites.title: Hindu Temple Society of North America

Visitors should dress moderately. No mini skirts or shorts above knee level. No ripped jeans. If needed, a wrap-around cloth will be provided for $5 each. No photo or videography is allowed inside the Main Prayer Hall. No pets permitted.

In 2023, the main building’s iconic Main Court and renowned Sorolla Gallery reopened to the public, the first step in a multi-phase restoration and revitalization project led by Beyer Blinder Belle Architects & Planners. Work continues to restore the building’s facades, terraces, and additional gallery and storage spaces.

Jennifer Whisenhunt and Graham Roscoe, Senior Associates from Beyer Blinder Belle, will lead a behind-the-scenes tour of the restoration and renovation of the campus and will visit the Terrace, East Gallery, Main Court, and Sorolla Gallery.

sites.name: Historic Cottage at Fort Tryon Park
sites.description:
Just across from the 190th Street A train stop, explore one of Upper Manhattan’s hidden treasures: the historic Cottage at Fort Tryon Park. Originally built as the gatehouse for the grand Billings Estate, this unique structure became part of the park when the land was transformed into public space in the early 1930s.

Today, the Cottage serves as the headquarters for NYC Parks’ Northern Manhattan Parks division and the Fort Tryon Park Conservancy—but for one special day during OHNY Weekend, its doors will be open for the public to explore.

Take a self-guided look around this rarely opened building, get a glimpse into the past, and learn about the history of the cottage, the surrounding neighborhood, and how Fort Tryon Park came to be.

Friendly guides will be on hand throughout the day to share stories and answer questions. Don’t miss this unique opportunity to connect with local history in one of NYC’s most beautiful parks.
sites.short: Step inside a rarely opened historic cottage for self-guided exploration, discover its origins as a grand estate gatehouse, and hear stories about local history and the area's transformation.

Lines are expected at this location. Last entry is 30 minutes prior to closing.

Rutan House (aka Rutan-Becket House), with its intact 1950s-era kitchen. 

The maritime past of Staten Island’s South Shore will be highlighted by these wonderful historic structures.

sites.name: Historic Neir's Tavern
sites.description:
Historic Neir's Tavern is the oldest continuously operating bar in NYC. There’s been a tavern on this spot since 1829, when it was called the Blue Pump Room. The tavern was re-named Neir’s Social Hall in 1898 when the Neir family took over ownership. Current owner Loycent Gordon is known far and wide as the man who saved Neir’s Tavern when he bought the bar in 2009 and restored it to what it is today. Along with the support of the community and the grassroots Neir’s Ambassadors’ Club, the bar was actually saved twice, and survived the pandemic as well. 

This year’s annual Block Party will mark Neir's 197th Anniversary on the “Road to 200,” which will be celebrated in 2029. Visitors can take a small group tour, personally guided by owner Loy Gordon, and/or his Executive Assistant, Kim, who will share history and the highlights before the bar opens to the public. Visitors will hear stories of how Mae West, Anthony Bourdain, Ray Liotta, and others came to be a part of Neir's lore. 

In addition to classic bar fare (available for purchase), Neir's menu features the “Goodfella” Burger, a proprietary recipe, and “The Wise Guy” signature cocktail, both of which are a nod to the fact that 14% of the iconic movie “Goodfellas” was filmed on-location at Neir’s.
sites.short: Join a small group tour led by the owner of the oldest continuously operating bar in NYC before opening hours to learn about the bar’s dramatic survival, then stick around to enjoy menu items inspired by the establishment's role in “Goodfellas.”

sites.name: Historic Richmond Town
sites.description:
Historic Richmond Town interprets and restores a living history village, operates a historical museum, and collects and preserves material culture to inspire engagement with and understanding of the diverse histories of Staten Island. 

On Saturday, October 17, OHNY Weekend participants can visit during Old Home Day, Historic Richmond Town's annual festival of living history and cultural heritage, showcasing the traditions of the past and the diversity of Staten Island today.

On Sunday, October 18, stop by for curator-led tours of a two-gallery exhibit, “Founding Principles: The Declaration of Independence, Civics, and Staten Island,” which uses local historical examples and objects from the collection, such as campaign buttons and items from 1776, to examine the different levels and branches of government as well as how citizens engage with government.
sites.short: Experience hands-on history with live demonstrations and cultural heritage activities, or join curator-led tours of a special exhibit featuring rare artifacts and local stories that explore Staten Island’s role in American civics and the founding of the nation.

While some of the site's buildings have wheelchair-accessible entrances, such as the Museum and Visitor Center at the 3rd County Courthouse, wheelchair access to many of the historic structures on site varies. For questions about site accessibility or requests for accommodation, contact the Visitor Services Department at (718)351-1611 ext. 247.

sites.name: Historic Tanker Ship MARY A. WHALEN
sites.description:
The MARY A. WHALEN is the last of her kind in the United States, is on the National Register of Historic Places, and is significant for a Supreme Court decision and more. She's also a handsome ship! As a coastal oil tanker, she is a great platform for discussing the history of American fuel consumption. 

Today, the ship is used for education and cultural programs (not a restoration of how the ship was outfitted in 1938). Visitors can go in the engine room and all interior spaces and can touch everything except the electrical panel, get on bunks, sit on the galley stools, and interact with the ship—there's no plexiglass or rope to hold you back! OHNY Weekend is one of the few times a year that the interior of the ship is open to the public because it is home to the offices of nonprofit PortSide NewYork.

Visitors get to explore the ship at their own pace. Docents will be stationed around the ship so no one feels rushed. A virtual guide to Red Hook past and present is also located at [www.redhookwaterstories.org](http://www.redhookwaterstories.org/)
sites.short: Step aboard the MARY A. WHALEN, the last of her kind in the USA, and explore this historic coastal oil tanker—now used for education and cultural programs—with no plexiglass or rope to hold you back!
sites.access_notes:
It is possible, although difficult, for people using walkers or wheelchairs to cross the gangway to the deck, but accessing the interior requires the use of stairs. Closed-toe, flat, rubber-soled shoes are strongly recommended, as the ship’s deck can be slippery and the gangway and some interior floors are metal grating. 

The available restrooms are portasans. There is a cat on-site.

Additional information about visiting the Mary A. Whalen can be found at <https://portsidenewyork.org/visitor-info>.

sites.name: Illuminating Black History in Brooklyn Tour
sites.description:
Bed-Stuy is not just Brooklyn's largest neighborhood—it is one of the most consequential sites of Black urban life in American history. This walking tour reveals what maps and real estate listings obscure: a community that has continuously built, owned, organized, and created culture despite more than a century of coordinated dispossession.

In honor of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and the 400th anniversary of the first enslaved Africans arriving on Lenape land, this Afrofuturist tour will take visitors through time from 1526 Lenapehoking through Weeksville, the Great Migration, the birth of hip hop, and into the future of this vibrant and changing neighborhood through its active sites of community resistance using augmented reality monuments developed by Kinfolk Tech.

GrowHouse Community Design + Development Group has been rooted in Bed-Stuy since 2017. Their work sits at the intersection of land sovereignty, civic design, and Black cultural memory. This tour is what GrowHouse does every day, made visible. The organization's walking tours began while organizing at the Flatbush African Burial Ground and have evolved to connect sites of Black history to contemporary businesses. GrowHouse has trained other organizations to lead tours, including fellow OHNY Weekend partner Friends of Abolitionist Place.

The tour is led by Shanna Sabio, Co-Founding Director of GrowHouse, and Faith Robinson, creator of Bed Stuy Forever.
sites.short: Experience Bed-Stuy’s rich legacy of Black resilience and creativity on a walking tour that highlights rarely seen sites and stories shaped by local organizers and uses augmented reality monuments to connect centuries of community resistance.

sites.partner: NYC Economic Development Corporation, Debra Simon Art Consulting, and WXY Studio
sites.description:
The Public Art at BAT program is fundamentally rooted in honoring and integrating Brooklyn Army Terminal’s (BAT) rich military past, present role as a modern industrial and creative hub, and its potential future. Today, BAT gets much of its character from its tenants and connection to New York City’s working waterfront. Most critically, the sheer number of tenants working within the complex—a diverse ecosystem of more than 3,500 visionaries, entrepreneurs, advanced manufacturers, makers, local workers, and artists—forms an engine of contemporary innovation.  

Public Art at BAT celebrates this concentration of creative and entrepreneurial energy. It treats the space of the terminal and surrounding public spaces as a massive canvas that reflects this industrious spirit. By commissioning sixteen site-responsive works, the program uncovers, interprets, and celebrates layers of history, commerce, and creativity, embedding the arts as a vital, permanent part of the terminal’s ongoing narrative. Each piece reflects the lived experience of the fourteen Brooklyn-based artists who have been engaged across these sites, many of whom are current or former BAT tenants themselves.

The tour is led by Debra Simon, Public Art Curator, and Olivia Jia, Senior Planner at WXY.

sites.description:
Inspiration Point is a nonprofit cultural arts center in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx, dedicated to supporting artists, presenting dynamic arts programming, and fostering inclusive community engagement through the arts. By providing space, resources, and opportunities for creative expression across disciplines, Inspiration Point embodies a commitment to accessibility, equity, and cultural vitality. 

Built on the site of the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Center, the multidisciplinary art space was established in 2023 and includes artist, residency, and specialty studios, galleries, FASHION MODA MODERN, the Off-Bruckner Theater Company, and the Tiffany Street Theater.

FASHION MODA MODERN is a revival of the groundbreaking South Bronx gallery founded by Stefan Eins in 1978. For fifteen years, Fashion Moda served as an interdisciplinary art space, fusing street culture, fine arts, and community engagement until its closing in 1993. The alternative art space challenged the elitism of the traditional art world, connecting the downtown art scene with the South Bronx, and conventional artistic disciplines with emerging urban mediums.

sites.description:
Get an expert-led preview of the the Interborough Express (IBX) on this tour highlighting Trains, Cranes & (Fewer) Automobiles. 

The IBX is a planned light rail line that will connect Brooklyn and Queens along an existing freight rail corridor. This project is currently in the planning phase and has the potential to bring changes to parts of both boroughs that are not currently well-served by public transportation.

Led by Moses Gates, Vice President for Housing and Neighborhood Planning at Regional Plan Association (the organization that originally conceptualized the IBX), this one-mile walk will take place on the streets alongside a section of the route near the Bensonhurst/Borough Park border. Participants will explore the opportunities and challenges associated with the project, including the balance between moving people and freight, the future of jobs and industry along the corridor, and the role this investment could play in shaping surrounding neighborhoods.

Participants are encouraged to wear comfortable walking shoes and be prepared for the weather.

sites.name: Ismaili Jamatkhana
sites.description:
Built in 1854, the five-story brick structure at 160 East 35th Street originally housed the city’s oldest police station, the 15th Precinct house. Most recently, the property was owned by Yeshiva University and used as classroom space for its Stern College for Women and Teachers Institute for Women. Thereafter, the building was established as a Jamatkhana—a place of gathering and worship—and an ambassadorial building for the work of its various institutions.   

The Ismaili Jamatkhana of Manhattan is a place of gathering for prayer but also a space for intellectual discourse. The interior spaces display elements of Islamic design and architectural elements of Jamatkhanas throughout the world. Through activities including lectures, seminars, exhibitions, and cultural and social events, the Ismaili Jamatkhana will create an understanding of the values, ethics, culture, and heritage of the Ismaili Muslims and of the work of the Aga Khan Development Network. It will also be an important space for the search for mutual understanding amongst all communities and cultures.
sites.short: Tour a place of gathering and worship, with unique architecture and interior elements of Islamic design, while learning about the values, ethics, culture, and heritage of the Ismaili Muslims.
