sites.name: Jack Shainman Gallery
sites.description:
The Jack Shainman Gallery on Lafayette Street is a major adaptive reuse renovation of the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission-designated New York Life Insurance Company Building (1894-1898), a monumental neo-Italian Renaissance tower. Initially designed by Stephen Decatur Hatch, construction supervision for the project was transferred to McKim, Mead & White after Hatch’s unexpected death in 1894. Mid-project, McKim, Mead & White’s Henry Bacon reconceptualized the original design: rather than incorporating the earlier New York Life Insurance Company headquarters, located at the west side of the block into the new building, Bacon arrived at a more uniform monolithic structure replacing the older building entirely.

Renovated in 1923 to include a mezzanine at the clerestory level of the General Office, also known as the Banking Hall, the landmark structure is notable for its luxurious marble, bronze and gilded finishes, impressive staircases and classically styled mahogany paneled interior spaces.

In 2024, after several years of restoration and renovation, Jack Shainman Gallery opened its doors to its new Tribeca flagship. Visiting the space with Walter Biggs, the gallery’s Director of Operations, provides a rare glimpse into the sensitively repurposed grand 19th century bank hall and its adjacent historical offices, collectively reimagined as a contemporary art gallery.
sites.short: Visit this flagship Tribeca gallery in a sensitively restored 19th-century neo-Italian Renaissance landmark, originally designed by Stephen Decatur Hatch and completed by McKim, Mead & White.

sites.name: Jackie Robinson Museum
sites.description:
On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson became the first African American to play Major League Baseball in the modern era. Off the field, he championed civil rights as an activist, advanced economic empowerment as a businessman, advocated for American ideals as an engaged citizen, and instilled core values as a family man.

The Jackie Robinson Museum celebrates the enduring legacy of one of the most important Americans of the 20th century, chronicling his trailblazing achievements against the backdrop of United States history. During OHNY Weekend, visit the museum with free admission from 11 AM–6 PM on Saturday, October 17, to learn about the legacy and impact of Jackie and Rachel Robinson through one-of-a-kind artifacts, interactive media, and multilayered storytelling.

sites.name: Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge West Pond
sites.partner: Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy and National Park Service
sites.description:
Join the Gateway National Recreation Area, the Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy, and the Science and Resilience Institute at Jamaica Bay for an immersive walking tour of the West Pond Living Shoreline at the Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge.

Learn how nature-based solutions and adaptive management are helping protect one of New York City's most important coastal ecosystems. Since its installation in 2021, the West Pond Living Shoreline has served as a living laboratory, where nature-based solutions are continuously tested, monitored, and adapted restoration techniques to improve shoreline resilience. Visitors will learn how the project has evolved from the installation of tree fascines constructed from salvaged Christmas trees to the next generation of restoration: Fascines 2.0. Developed through a collaborative pilot project led by the Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy, Fascines 2.0 is an innovative solution that combines woody fascines with habitat features designed to encourage ribbed mussel recruitment. Together, these living shoreline elements help dissipate wave energy, trap sediment, stabilize marsh edges, create habitat, and strengthen the resilience of the shoreline over time.

As part of the tour led by JBRPC Stewardship Programs Manager Anil Pasram, visitors will have the opportunity to see one of the pilot installations and learn how ongoing monitoring and research are informing the future of coastal restoration in Jamaica Bay. Through collaboration, experimentation, and adaptive management, this project is helping shape more resilient shorelines that can better withstand rising seas and increasingly frequent coastal storms. This tour offers a unique opportunity to experience how science, innovation, and stewardship are coming together to restore one of New York City's most important natural landscapes.
sites.short: Explore an innovative living shoreline project where nature-based solutions are tested to protect and restore coastal ecosystems, with exclusive access to pilot installations and insights into ongoing research shaping the future of shoreline resilience.

address.note: The James Gallery at The Graduate Center, CUNY.

sites.description:
ART/WORK: The Practice and Politics of CETA and the Arts, 1974–1981, is the first major exhibition to examine the national impact of the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act (CETA), a federal jobs program that placed more than 30,000 cultural workers on local government payrolls in nearly 200 cities, towns, and Indigenous territories.

Though largely absent from public memory today, between 1974 and 1981, CETA reshaped cultural infrastructure nationwide, supporting arts workers in civic, experimental, and community-rooted contexts while expanding public access to cultural participation.

Through case studies spanning New York City, Atlanta, Baltimore, Chicago, Kingston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington, D.C., and Whitesburg, KY, ART/WORK reconstructs this forgotten chapter of American cultural history while asking a timely question: What becomes possible when artists are treated as essential workers and cultural labor is understood as a public good?

ART/WORK is on view at the James Gallery, located on the ground floor of the CUNY Graduate Center in Midtown Manhattan. Operating closely with the Graduate Center’s PhD Program in Art History, the gallery is a unique exhibition space that centers student training and pedagogy at every level of its operation. Its mission is to bring artists and scholars into public dialogue through exhibitions, research, and public programs.

The exhibition will remain open on Friday, October 16, from 4-8 PM for OHNY Weekend, with tours led by curators Jodi Waynberg and Molly Garfinkel.
sites.short: The exhibition _ART/WORK_ at CUNY's James Gallery examines the impact of the federal Comprehensive Employment and Training Act from 1974 to 1981, which employed over 30,000 artists to reshape American cultural infrastructure.

Beginning at BronxArtSpace and culminating at the Enslaved African Burial Ground in Drake Park, participants will engage in a combination of storytelling, archival exploration, and sensory exercises to unearth the often hidden history of Northern slavery. Together, the tour group will reflect on the past while drawing connections to environmental justice, mass incarceration, and displacement. The tour concludes with a libation ritual at the Burial Ground, inviting participants to honor the memories of those buried at the site. 

The walk is led by Alethea Pace, an interdisciplinary performing artist and educator. Her work weaves movement, storytelling, oral history, and community engagement to foster connections between people, place, and memory. Through this embodied experience, visitors will gain a new understanding of Hunts Point's rich history while initiating a dialogue around more just futures.

sites.name: Kingsborough Houses: “Exodus & Dance” and “Migration”
sites.partner: New York City Housing Authority and Public Housing Community Fund
sites.description:
At the heart of NYCHA’s Kingsborough Houses in Brooklyn stands Exodus and Dance, a monumental frieze created in 1941 by Harlem Renaissance sculptor Richmond Barthé. Completed during the WPA era under the Federal Art Project, the relief is a rare example of public art in public housing reflecting themes of resilience, spirituality, and joy. For decades, the piece weathered the elements, its details fading from view—until a major restoration effort brought it back to life. Between December 2023 and July 2025, NYCHA and the Public Housing Community Fund partnered with Jemco Electrical Contractors, EverGreene Architectural Arts, Ronnette Riley Architect, Jablonski Building Conservation, and Fisher Marantz Stone to carefully conserve and relight the work. Visitors will see the frieze newly illuminated in its full brilliance, learn the story of Barthé—one of the most important Black sculptors of the 20th century—and explore how WPA-era public art and New Deal housing intersect.

The tour will also highlight a new permanent public art installation and heritage walk, "Migration." Installed across the development’s 16-acre campus, the 35 illuminated steel artworks draw inspiration from Egyptian and African diasporic motifs, the new Exodus and Dance frieze, and the memories and experiences of Kingsborough residents themselves. Created by Jerome Haferd Studios and Creative Urban Alchemy in collaboration with Kingsborough Houses residents, local artists, and cultural historians, the installation transforms daily pathways into places of reflection and gathering. Workshops with residents shaped the inscriptions and designs, ensuring the walk reflects the stories, aspirations, and resilience of the Kingsborough community.

This OHNY Weekend tour offers a rare chance to experience world-class art in a public housing community—where history, creativity, and community pride come together.
sites.short: Experience the newly restored 1940s frieze, illuminated for the first time in decades, and explore a unique heritage walk featuring 35 steel artworks inspired by African diasporic motifs and residents’ stories.

sites.description: The LES Ecology Center's Tool Lending Library presents an Urban Forest Fall Celebration! Visit the Clyde Romero Memorial Garden in the East Village to discover how the center supports the community in stewarding the urban forest, and how you too can care for your friendly neighborhood trees. Learn why trees are a green infrastructure that is key to urban climate resiliency, try out a variety of tree care tools from the library, enjoy tree pruning demos, create colorful tree bed signs, and plant daffodil bulbs.
sites.short: Join a hands-on celebration to learn about urban forest stewardship and put the lessons to work, caring for plants in an East Village community garden.
sites.access_notes: All activities take place outside, in a wheelchair-accessible space. Kneeling might be required for some activities. Closed-toe shoes, long sleeved-shirts, pants and hats are recommended. Gloves and all other necessary tools and gear will be provided.
sites.special:
**Sunday Activities:**
- Daffodil bulb planting at 11 AM and 12 PM
- Pruning demonstrations at 12:30 and 1:30 PM

sites.name: Lewis Latimer House
sites.description:
Lewis Latimer was the son of self-emancipated Virginians who grew up to contribute to the development of the light bulb. He was a self-taught patent expert and inventor who also patented seven devices, including an early air conditioning system! He was also a soulful creative who wrote poems and shared his love of the arts with his two daughters, who were practicing artists during the Harlem Renaissance.  

Visit Latimer's home in Flushing, Queens, to learn more about the incredible story of the inventor and his family through the permanent exhibition, "Light Up the World: The Legacy of Lewis H. Latimer." Visitors will also be able to explore exhibition interactives, including a selfie printing station.
sites.short: Explore the remarkable legacy of a self-taught inventor and his artistic family through interactive exhibits, a photo printing station, and engaging scavenger hunts.
sites.access_notes:
Multilingual museum content can be accessed before and during a visit through the free, Bloomberg Connects digital guide. 

Food is not allowed in the museum galleries.
sites.family: **Family Friendly**: Explore the "Light Up the World: The Legacy of Lewis H. Latimer" permanent exhibition as part of a guided or self-guided tour and participate in a fall-themed, family-friendly scavenger hunt. Then, explore exhibition interactives including: the "Invention Machine," featuring digital versions of Lewis Latimer's seven patent, and snap and print a photo using the "Inventor Selfie Filter" interactive!
sites.special: **Saturday & Sunday Tours: **First tour 12:15 and last tour 3:15 PM; tours every hour

sites.name: LIC Boathouse and East River CREW
sites.partner: LIC Community Boathouse and East River CREW
sites.description: During OHNY Weekend, LIC Boathouse and East River CREW invites participants to step back in time and row an authentic replica Whitehall Gig in Long Island City. Visitors will learn to maneuver these historic vessels, experiencing the living history of the very waters where they ruled 19th-century maritime life. Before gasoline engines, the Whitehall rowboat—perfected at the foot of Whitehall Street in Lower Manhattan—was the ultimate workhorse of New York Harbor. By taking the oars, history buffs can step into the shoes of the 1800s water taxis, harbor police, ship pilots, and newspaper reporters who once rushed to meet incoming ships.
sites.short: Row a replica 19th-century Whitehall Gig and experience firsthand the historic techniques used by harbor workers while learning about New York’s maritime past on the very waters these boats once ruled.

websites.title: LIC Community Boathouse and East River CREW

sites.access_notes:
All visitors must sign a liability waiver to participate. The dock is accessed by a ladder and is not wheelchair accessible. 

Flat, rubber-soled, closed-toe shoes are required to participate (no flip flops). Participants should dress for the weather and wear protective clothing (windbreaker, rain jacket, etc.) as necessary. A phone case is highly recommended to keep your phone attached and protected from wetness.

Please plan to arrive on time for your session. The boats have a minimum as well as a maximum capacity to operate effectively.

Visitors must be 18+.

sites.name: Little Island After Dark
sites.partner: Fisher Marantz Stone and Little Island
sites.description:
A daring partnership between the Diller-von Furstenberg Family Foundation and Hudson River Park Trust, Little Island was born from the unique opportunity to envision a solution for the repair and renovation of Pier 54, and to reimagine an entirely new type of public space for New York City, one that would create an immersive experience with nature and art. 

In the evening, visitors first notice the festively illuminated park from a distance, while strolling along the Hudson River Park Esplanade, which runs from Chambers to West 59th Street. The historic Cunard-White Star Line Arch, newly restored and sparkling with light, acts as an entry beacon leading to the luminous bridge and the uplit concrete pots supporting the park. Once onsite, the visitor can explore the various highlighted paths, ramps, and stairs, take in a show in the Amphitheater, or simply marvel at the unparalleled views of New York City, the Hudson River, and New Jersey.

During OHNY Weekend, spend an hour with Fisher Marantz Stone lighting designer Amy Leder on an early evening tour to discuss the lighting vision for this unique space.
sites.short: Join a special evening tour led by the park’s lighting designer to explore its innovative illumination, restored historic arch, and dramatic views while learning about the creative lighting concepts behind this immersive public space.
sites.access_notes:
Little Island is fully accessible and has paved pathways. Restrooms are located near The Glade just past the South Bridge entrance to the park. Please no pets, except for service animals.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.
accessibility: Drinking fountain or water bottle filling station

sites.name: LiveOnNY Kidney Rescue Area & Sim Center
sites.description:
Somewhere behind every transplant is a race against time. A recovered kidney has only hours to travel from donor to recipient, and in that narrow window, a team of specialists works to evaluate, preserve, and protect it, ensuring the donor's final act of generosity reaches the person waiting for it.

This tour takes participants inside LiveOnNY's Kidney Rescue and Simulation Center, the state-of-the-art facility where that work happens. Recovered kidneys are brought to the Rescue Area, where they're assessed and cared for prior to transplant, part of a process that blends clinical precision with something more human: the ongoing legacy of a donor's gift.

Participants will get a full overview of how organ and tissue donation works, from recovery to transplant, before stepping into a fully equipped mock Operating Room and Intensive Care Unit, the same spaces used to train LiveOnNY's clinical staff for the moments that matter most. The tour also includes firsthand stories from transplant recipients and family members of LiveOnNY donors, whose experiences bring the science back down to something deeply personal.

Led by LiveOnNY's clinical and donor services team, the tour translates the science and systems behind organ donation into something participants can see, understand, and carry with them. By the end, the phrase "gift of life" won't just be a phrase. It'll be a place one has stood inside.
sites.short: Step into a mock operating room and ICU at a cutting-edge organ donation center to explore real-life recovery and transplant processes.
sites.access_notes:
Visitors must show valid photo ID for entry. Tickets are transferable.

Multilingual translation and printed materials available in Cantonese, Mandarin, Hindi, Punjabi, and Spanish. To request translation services, email info@ohny.org by October 12. 

Children 15+ welcome. Every person attending, including children, must have a ticket.
accessibility: Drinking fountain or water bottle filling station

sites.name: Look Up! A NYC Water Tower Tour
sites.description:
For over 100 years, wooden water towers have stood above New York City as emblems of ingenuity and resiliency. Familiar yet often overlooked, these structures are an undisputed anchor of the skyline and a distinctly New York icon.

During OHNY Weekend, join NYC Tour Guide Abby Ross for a walking tour highlighting these structures: learn how they work, their role in the city's growth, and why they remain relevant today. The tour will discuss how water towers have appeared in art and architecture through the decades and celebrate their place as a symbol of New York. After the guided tour, visitors can keep exploring with a Look Up, New York Water Tower Map.
sites.short: Dive into the hidden history and enduring significance of New York's iconic wooden water towers on a guided walking tour, featuring insights into their engineering, cultural impact, and continued relevance, plus a special map for further self-guided discovery.
sites.access_notes:
There is an elevator up to the High Line on 23rd & 10th Avenue. 

This is an outdoor walking tour taking place in public areas and city streets. Dress for the weather and wear comfortable shoes.

Children 13+ welcome. Every person attending, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Lotus Garden

address.note: Enter at the south side of West 97th between Broadway and West End Avenue.

sites.description: Designed by Carrie Maher and Mark Greenwald in 1984 and perched atop a brick condo tower’s parking garage, this oasis in the sky features varied flowers, fruit trees, shrubs, and lotus ponds inhabited by colorful goldfish. The 1/6th-acre paradise, with three feet of dirt underfoot and multiple birds’ nests tucked overhead, is among the city’s oldest rooftop gardens. Run entirely by volunteers, the Lotus Garden wows people who climb the short flight of stairs with its colorful and fragrant abundance, surprisingly wedged between apartment buildings.
sites.short: Discover an urban oasis hiding in plain sight and filled with vibrant flowers, fruit trees, and namesake lotus ponds with goldfish, all maintained by dedicated volunteers.
sites.access_notes:
Visitors must go up one flight of stairs to access the garden. 

The garden paths are mulched and may be uneven. Closed-toe, non-heeled shoes are strongly recommended.
sites.special:
**Sunday Tours:** Ongoing 10 AM–2 PM
Experienced gardeners will be on-site to give first-come, first-served tours that explain the site's past, present, and future—what has been planted, why, how it has evolved, and how it is maintained.

sites.name: Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House
sites.description:
Spend your Saturday afternoon in the Lower East Side exploring over 20 arts & culture organizations! Organized by Fourth Arts Block (FABnyc), the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House is now in its fourth year, welcoming folks into cultural spaces without a ticket to a show or the cost of admission. All organizations will have staff available to answer questions about their programs, and many will offer special free activities such as tours, exhibits, workshops, and performances!

Begin on the East 4th Street Open Street and get to know the East 4th Street Cultural District; the only officially designated cultural district in Manhattan, founded by grassroots arts & community organizations to rally against their own displacement from the neighborhood. Through collective advocacy and with community support, groups successfully purchased six buildings and two vacant lots from the city, for $1 each, all deed-restricted to nonprofit cultural use. Today the District houses 14 arts groups, 10 cultural facilities, and 22 performance and rehearsal venues, and has more active cultural space per square foot than any other block in New York City.  

On 4th Street, you’ll grab maps & plan your route, check out live music & hands-on arts activities good for all ages, and meet folks from ABC No Rio, Bond Street Theater, Cooper Square Actors Center, FABnyc, IATI Theater, International Center of Photography, La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club, Lower East Side Preservation Initiative, Magnum Foundation, New York Theatre Workshop, Nuyorican Poets Cafe, Poetry Project, Swiss Institute and WOW Cafe Theatre all right there on the block!

Then, with a map in hand, you’ll venture out into the historic Lower East Side to visit Abrons Arts Center, Artists Alliance Inc., The Clemente Soto Velez Cultural & Educational Center, International Center for Photography, Loisaida Inc., Movement Research, The Performance Project @ University Settlement, Think!Chinatown, and the Ukrainian Museum. They’ll all be opening their doors for you to explore free exhibits, visit artists' studios, participate in workshops, and more!
sites.short: Explore over 20 arts and culture organizations with free access to exhibits, performances, workshops, and behind-the-scenes activities, including rare opportunities to visit artists' studios and meet staff from renowned cultural groups.
sites.access_notes:
Multiple sites are open during the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House. Accessibility services vary by site. Please refer to each site's specific info in your planning.

The 'hub' for the LES Arts & Culture Open House is on the East 4th Street Open Street -- be prepared to spend some time outside. Some sites may have photography restrictions depending on the exhibit or showing.

sites.name: Lower East Side Printshop
sites.description: Lower East Side Printshop is a nonprofit printmaking studio, established in 1968 by artist and educator Eleanor Magid. Now located in Midtown West, the Printshop continues its mission to help artists explore printmaking media, and advance their artistic career through residencies, internships, classes, and exhibitions. During OHNY Weekend, visit for a studio tour, see a residency artists' exhibition, and meet artists in the studio to learn more about the Printshop's community and how it supports contemporary artists.
sites.short: Tour the Midtown home of an historic printmaking studio, view a special exhibition of residency artists' work, and meet artists in person to learn how the space supports contemporary creators.
sites.access_notes: The Printshop has a no pet policy in the studios. Please request a service animal waiver in the office prior to entry.

sites.name: M&S Schmalberg Flowers
sites.description:
Step inside M&S Schmalberg, the last remaining fabric flower manufacturer in the United States. Founded in 1916, this family-run workshop has been handcrafting custom flowers in the Garment District for over a century using many of the same vintage tools, dies, and techniques passed down through four generations.

During OHNY Weekend, participants will see how fabric flowers are made from start to finish: cutting fabric with antique steel dies, shaping petals with heated irons, hand-dyeing materials, and assembling each flower by hand.

M&S Schmalberg flowers have appeared everywhere from high fashion runways and Broadway costumes to film, television, weddings, and museum exhibitions. At its core, M&S Schmalberg remains a working factory, producing everything by hand in the same Manhattan studio where prior generations have done the same.

This is a chance to experience a living craft, meet the makers, and see firsthand how a small family business continues to preserve an art form that has nearly vanished from the city.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes at a historic, family-run workshop to watch hand-crafted fabric flowers made with century-old tools and techniques, meet the artisans, and witness a rare living tradition in action.
sites.access_notes:
The site is generally wheelchair accessible, though some areas have narrow aisles and limited space. Visitors with specific inquiries or accommodation requests should email info@ohny.org by October 12.

M&S Schmalberg is an active working factory, so visitors should expect a functioning production environment with machinery, heat tools, and occasional noise. Closed-toe shoes are recommended.
accessibility: Drinking fountain or water bottle filling station
sites.family: **Family Friendly:** Kids will love seeing how fabric is transformed into flowers using real vintage molds and machines — it’s like stepping into a fairy tale. M&S Schmalberg even made flowers for Rapunzel! The studio is full of color, texture, and creativity — and guides are happy to offer hands-on moments for little ones.

sites.name: MADE Bush Terminal
sites.partner: NYC Economic Development Corporation and Turnstile Tours
sites.description:
MADE Bush Terminal (Manufacturers, Artisans, Designers, Entrepreneurs) is an ambitious urban redevelopment project in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, transforming a historic 36-acre waterfront property into a modern, mixed-use hub for local producers, fabricators, and creatives. 

Managed by the NYC Economic Development Corporation on behalf of the City, the project's core mission is to foster economic growth through local job creation, community engagement, and sustainable development while preserving the area's rich industrial heritage. By providing affordable spaces, job opportunities, public amenities, and innovative retail programming, MADE Bush Terminal seeks to create a dynamic ecosystem where innovation, creativity, and tradition coexist, benefiting both businesses and the immediate local community.

Learn about MADE’s past, present, and future with complimentary tours and explore new public gathering and select tenant spaces on OHNY Weekend.
sites.short: Discover a mixed-use hub for local producers, fabricators, and creatives on the Brooklyn waterfront: a dynamic ecosystem where innovation, creativity, and tradition coexist.

sites.description:
MakerSpace NYC is a 40,000-square-foot fabrication facility for artists, designers, craftspeople, makers, and manufacturers, spanning two spaces at the Brooklyn Army Terminal. During OHNY Weekend, visitors can tour the main facility in Building B for industrial machine demonstrations, and the pottery studio in Building A for pottery demonstrations and member exhibitions.

Meet a variety of makers and see tools such as the induction forge and pottery wheel in action.
sites.short: Tour expansive fabrication spaces, meet skilled makers, and watch live demonstrations of industrial machines and pottery techniques.

sites.name: Mama Joy's Abolitionist Walking Tour
sites.description: Join local historian Raul Rothblatt and community educator Shawne Lee for an immersive public history experience that explores Downtown Brooklyn's rich legacy of Black freedom, abolition, and resistance. Inspired by the work of preservationist Mama Joy Chatel, this tour guides participants through historic sites connected to the Underground Railroad and the individuals who fought for freedom and justice. Through storytelling, historical interpretation, and community memory, visitors gain a deeper understanding of Brooklyn's vital role in the struggle for Black liberation. Come curious, leave changed!
sites.short: Explore Downtown Brooklyn’s pivotal sites of Black freedom and abolition with expert guides, uncovering Underground Railroad history and personal stories of resistance through engaging storytelling and community memory.
sites.access_notes:
This is an outdoor walking tour. Participants should dress for the weather, wear comfortable shoes, and bring water. Seating is available at the tour meeting point.

The nearest restroom is located in City Point, close to the tour's starting and ending locations.

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Meatpacking District Walking Tour
sites.description:
Explore the evolution of New York City’s Meatpacking District through four projects by Morris Adjmi Architects that reflect the neighborhood’s transformation from an industrial hub into one of the city’s most dynamic destinations.

Led by Christopher Courtney, Project Manager, and Emily Contreras, Events & Social Media Manager, of the MA team, this walking tour will visit the Theory Building (40 Gansevoort Street), 837 Washington Street, 414 West 14th Street, and the High Line Building (450 W 14th Street), each offering a different perspective on designing within and around the Gansevoort Market Historic District. Together, the projects demonstrate how new architecture can respond to historic context while supporting the changing needs of the neighborhood.

Along the way, the tour will explore MA’s approach to adaptive reuse, restoration, and new construction, with a focus on the materials, forms, and industrial character that define the Meatpacking District. Participants will also learn how the firm has worked within the neighborhood’s landmark framework to preserve its distinct identity while contributing to its continued evolution.

Spanning different moments in the Meatpacking District’s transformation, these four projects offer a glimpse into the role architecture can play in shaping change while maintaining a meaningful connection to the past.
sites.short: Join an architect-led walk to explore four significant projects that showcase how innovative design, adaptive reuse, and restoration have transformed one of the city's former industrial hubs while preserving its historic character.
sites.access_notes:
This is a walking tour in the Meatpacking District. The entire tour will be outside and will consist of a 0.5 mile walk, and the neighborhood has cobblestone streets. Please dress appropriately for the weather. Comfortable walking shoes recommended. 

Children are welcome, accompanied by an adult. All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Midnight Leak Detection with NYC DEP
sites.description:
Join the NYC Department of Environmental Protection for an inside look at the operations of the Leak Detection team and learn how their work protects New Yorkers’ water supply.

Each day, a billion gallons of drinking water travel through 7,000 miles of underground pipes in the five boroughs to New Yorkers’ taps. New York City has one of the most reliable water delivery systems in the country, and NYC DEP is hard at work to keep it that way. The Leak Detection team proactively canvasses to catch leaking water mains before they lead to major breaks, which can cause major disruptions to service.
 
Using stethoscope-like devices to listen to the streets, the Leak Detection Team pinpoints the location of leaks so repair teams can get to work. Working at night, when the city is comparatively quiet, the Leak Detection team can listen to 40,000 feet of water mains per shift.
 
On this midnight tour, participants will see the Leak Detection team in action and have the opportunity to listen to the water mains beneath our streets.
sites.short: Join a listening session with the City's Leak Detection team to witness their specialized techniques for identifying underground water main leaks and get a chance to hear the city’s water pipes in action.
sites.access_notes:
This program will take place entirely outdoors and participants will be standing throughout. Participants should dress for the weather and wear closed-toe shoes. Please do not bring anything other than a bag you can carry, as there is no place to securely leave items.

Visitors must be 18+.

sites.name: Mmuseumm
sites.description: Mmmuseumm is a space for telling stories about the modern world through "Object Journalism." Currently on view is the collection RUBBLE, which presents fragments from around the world. A talented, eclectic docent will be present to share any details or secrets about the collection and each piece's story.
sites.short: Discover a hidden gem displaying a unique collection of global fragments and uncover the stories behind each piece, guided by an engaging docent ready to share insights and secrets.
sites.access_notes: The museum exists in a former elevator shaft adjacent to the sidewalk. It is possible to enter in with a mobility device directly from the sidewalk, but may require entering the sidewalk at the end of the block.

sites.name: Monumental Labs
sites.description:
**This location has canceled. Drop-In access will not be offered on Sunday, October 18, due to construction delays at the site.**

Monumental Labs occupies a 40,000-square-foot fabrication facility in Greenpoint, the largest robotic stone carving operation in New York City. It is a working shop, closed to the public, where industrial robots and classically trained hand carvers cut stone for buildings across the city and the country.

For most of the last century, carved stone ornament was priced out of American construction. The craft did not disappear so much as it became unaffordable. Monumental Labs was founded to change that math. Robotic milling handles the geometric roughing that once consumed weeks of skilled labor. Carvers then finish the organic and sculptural passages by hand—the work no machine does well. The combination makes architectural stone viable again at a scale New York has not seen since before World War II.
sites.short: A cutting-edge stone carving facility, where industrial robots and skilled artisans transform raw stone into intricate architectural details.

sites.name: Morbid Anatomy Library
sites.description:
Visit the Morbid Anatomy Library in Industry City, Brooklyn, to view a collection of books and curiosities, along with a brand-new installation of nearly 50 pieces of Victorian Hair Work from the legendary Leila’s Hair Museum in Independence, Missouri.

Art made using human hair was a popular craft during the Victorian era, used to create intricate family trees and mementos of dead loved ones. In 1986, hairdresser and self-taught historian and maker Leila Cohoon founded Leila’s Hair Museum, the first and only museum devoted entirely to art made from human hair. By the time it closed upon her death in 2024, it housed over 3,000 works. Morbid Anatomy is honored to become one of the spiritual homes for this collection of family tree wreaths, memorial artworks, and intricate jewelry, each meticulously crafted from human hair.

During OHNY Weekend, visitors are invited to explore the hair art installation, browse shelves of image-rich books on death and culture, anatomical art, esoterica, and folklore, and wander among an idiosyncratic array of artifacts, specimens, devotional objects, and curiosities from around the world. The gift shop will be open, featuring rare and unusual items—from obscure tarot decks and antique Mexican retablos to handmade masks, jewelry, and carefully selected books.
sites.short: Explore a rare installation of nearly 50 intricate Victorian hair art pieces from the renowned Leila’s Hair Museum, browse unique books on death and culture, and discover an eclectic array of global curiosities and unusual gifts.
sites.access_notes: This is a library/museum setting. No food or drink are permitted inside, and noise levels should be kept at a minimum so as not to disturb reading visitors.

sites.name: Mount Morris Fire Watchtower
sites.partner: NYC Department of Parks and Recreation Urban Park Rangers

address.note: Entrance at the intersection of West 122nd Street & Mount Morris Park West.

sites.description:
This 1857 tower, the last of its kind, was designated a New York City Landmark in 1967 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976. While the fire tower network—which at its peak included 11 towers—fell into disuse in the 1870s, the bell atop the Mount Morris tower continued to sound for timekeeping and churchgoing purposes until about 1909. In 2000, architect and preservationist Angel Ayón, Principal of AYON Studio, began advising stakeholders, including the Mt. Morris Park Community Improvement Association and the Marcus Garvey Park Alliance, in their campaign to save the tower. As a result of their collective advocacy, the tower’s rehabilitation was completed by the City.

Tour the historic Mount Morris Fire Watchtower, a prominent feature of Marcus Garvey Park and its neighborhood. Get inside, ring the 5,000 lb. bell, and walk the spiral staircase to enjoy the views. Access is limited to 12 people at a time. Lines are expected, but please note that OHNY Weekend Passports do not provide expedited access at this location.
sites.short: Climb the spiral staircase of a beautifully restored 1857 fire watchtower to take in panoramic views and ring the original 5,000-pound bell.

sites.name: Movement Research
sites.description:
A globally-recognized laboratory for the investigation of dance and movement-based forms, Movement Research is located in the 122 Cultural Center located at the corner of First Avenue and Ninth Street. Movement Research’s spaces were designed by Angel Ayón, Lead Architect of AYON Studio. The 122CC is housed in a Romanesque Revival style building originally constructed as Public School 122, designed by renowned school architect Charles B.J. Snyder. In the 2010s, the building underwent a multiyear floor-to-ceiling renovation designed by Deborah Berke Partners. 

During OHNY Weekend, Movement Research will host tours of its dance studios and auxiliary spaces led by architect Angel Ayón and Movement Research staff. Drop-in sample class sessions will also be offered, exploring a variety of physical inquiry and somatic practices such as Alexander Technique and Feldenkrais®.  The materials, methodologies, and approaches of each session are informed by the unique creative investigations of each teaching artist. Visitors are welcome to come and explore these body and movement practices. Comfortable clothing that is easy to move in is recommended.
sites.short: Tour architect-designed dance studios and join drop-in sample classes in somatic practices guided by expert teaching artists and staff.
sites.access_notes:
Movement Research spaces are fragrance free to accommodate individuals with fragrance allergies and/or chemical sensitivities. Please refrain from wearing fragrances or manufactured scents on your visit. 

If participating in a movement session, comfortable clothing is recommended, and shoes will need to be removed; socks or barefoot are fine. A storage area for shoes is available. 

Auditive guidance is available if arranged in advance. To request accommodation, email info@ohny.org by October 12.

Please no pets, except for service animals.

sites.name: MS053 School-Based Hydroponic Farm
sites.partner: Teens for Food Justice and MS053
sites.description:
Inside MS053 in Far Rockaway is something most New Yorkers would never expect: a commercial-grade hydroponic farm, built right inside a public school building.

This farm grows lettuce, kale, herbs, and other crops year-round, indoors, using a soil-free system that runs on water and light instead of weather and seasons. It produces at a scale most people associate with commercial growers, not classrooms. The food grown here doesn't leave the community. It goes straight to the school cafeteria and to nearby families and neighbors, at no cost. Teens for Food Justice (TFFJ) built and operates the farm in partnership with the school, training district staff to run it as a working hydroponic operation.

On this tour, participants will see the full growing system up close: seedlings, mature crops, and the equipment that keeps it running. Staff will be on-site to answer questions about how the farm works, what gets grown, and how a system like this fits inside an existing public school building. Ticket holders may arrive up to 30 minutes after their session start time.

Most food production happens far from where people live. This farm puts it inside a school, in the middle of a dense urban neighborhood, where the people eating the food can also see it grown. Visit to learn how a public school building can also be a working farm, and how that changes what's possible for food access in this community.

Guests may arrive up to 30 minutes after their session start time.
sites.short: Discover a commercial-scale hydroponic farm built within a public school, where crops are grown year-round using an innovative soil-free system, transforming food access in the community.

sites.name: MTA 207th Street Yard
sites.description:
**Booking this experience is a two-step process**. Review the "Policies" section below for full details.

Tour participants will get a behind-the-scenes look at the flood mitigation infrastructure protecting the MTA's 207th St Yard, a critical facility for the New York City Subway system, located in Northern Manhattan alongside the Harlem River. It functions as the main storage yard for rolling stock on the A and C Lines and houses one of only two heavy overhaul shops in the system—the other being at Coney Island Yard in Brooklyn. The 207th Street Shop handles the overhaul and rebuilding of most B Division cars, as well as select A Division rolling stock, making it essential to the maintenance and reliability of subway operations.

Following significant damage sustained during Hurricane Sandy, a major flood protection project was launched to protect the yard and its infrastructure from future storm events. A central feature of this effort is a 1,535-linear-foot marine floodwall strategically positioned along the Harlem River. Engineered to withstand a 500-year flood event, the floodwall consists of 279 interconnected 54-inch diameter steel pipe piles, forming a robust barrier against rising waters. The project also includes the installation of grout curtains, stop logs, sliding gates, additional drains, and discharge pipes to manage water more effectively.

Beyond the marine floodwall, additional protective measures were implemented to further fortify the facility. These include a new upland perimeter wall, stainless steel and flexible flood gates at entry points, and the use of complex underwater lightweight concrete pours to seal off the existing relieving platform. The project also involved the demolition of adjacent structures and the construction of multiple cut-off walls to reinforce the yard’s foundation and prevent water intrusion. Together, these upgrades form a permanent and resilient flood defense system for one of the subway system’s most vital maintenance and storage hubs.
sites.short: Get a close look at resiliency upgrades and recently installed flood protection measures at this vital piece of transit infrastructure—one of two heavy overhaul shops in the system.

sites.description:
**Booking this experience is a two-step process**. Review the "Policies" section below for full details.

This project is transforming 42 St–Bryant Park station into a fully accessible station complex and strengthening accessibility along the 42nd Street corridor. MTA is constructing four new elevators: two connecting the Bryant Park mezzanine to the northbound and southbound B/D/F/M platforms, one connecting the Times Square Shuttle passageway to the Bryant Park complex, and one serving the 5th Avenue 7 train platform. 

Together with the complex’s existing street-to-mezzanine elevators, these improvements will create an accessible path through the station and an in-system accessible connection toward Times Square. 

The project scope extends well beyond the elevators, and includes upgrades to boarding areas, architectural finishes, lighting, signage, passenger information, and communications systems, as well as State of Good Repair repairs in public areas of both stations. 

The site visit will give participants a look "Behind the Blue Door" to see how this major subway accessibility project is designed and delivered within one of Midtown’s most complex transit environments.

sites.name: MTA Arts & Design: "In Service" by Christopher Payne
sites.description:
Join industrial photographer Christopher Payne for a special tour of “In Service: MTA Photographs by Christopher Payne,” the first “takeover” exhibition in MTA Arts & Design’s photography program. Known for his explorations of complex systems and the often unseen choreography of labor, Payne brings an extraordinary behind-the-scenes perspective to New York’s transit operations. This tour offers the rare opportunity to learn more about the stories behind the photographs and to hear directly from the artist about the curiosity and precision that drive his practice.

With exhibition curator Maggie Murtha, Manager, MTA Arts & Design, Payne will guide participants through three key exhibition sites. The tour begins at the Grand Central Madison lightboxes, where he will introduce this expansive project and discuss his history photographing the transit system. The group will then move to the gallery space in the Grand Central Dining Concourse for deeper insight into Payne’s photographic process, including the unique challenges of photographing active industrial environments and the collaboration required to access these spaces. Finally, the tour concludes at the 42 St–Bryant Park station lightboxes, showcasing additional works that reflect the artistry embedded in the system’s infrastructure that keeps the region moving.

Don’t miss this chance to see the exhibition in situ and learn directly from the artist and curator shaping this landmark presentation.
sites.short: Experience a behind-the-scenes tour of New York’s transit system through the lens of industrial photography, guided by the artist and exhibition curator, with insights into the creative process.

sites.description:
Join a tour of the extraordinary art installations from Grand Central to Times Square, led by MTA Arts & Design Deputy Directors, Yaling Chen and Cheryl Hageman. When the New York City Subway opened in 1904, its founders declared that the railway was a "great public work" where every design element should show respect for customers and enhance the experience of travel through beauty and efficiency. For more than 40 years, since 1985, MTA Arts & Design has continued to carry forward this belief by presenting breathtaking permanent and temporary works of art, bringing art everywhere, for everyone. 

The tour will begin at Grand Central and conclude at Times Square in Manhattan. Making stops along the way, attendees will see incredible artworks commissioned by leading contemporary artists including Yayoi Kusama, Kiki Smith, Jim Hodges, Samm Kunce, and Nick Cave. Tour participants will learn how these installations are made and hear the stories behind vibrant works that celebrate transit spaces and city life. Bring your own OMNY card. Extra swipes will not be needed as the tour moves from station to station. Comfortable shoes are encouraged.

sites.description:

The MTA is reconstructing and expanding the Jamaica Bus Depot in Queens. This project will modernize the depot and provide the facilities needed to operate, maintain, and store up to 300 buses. The original depot was built in 1939, and the facility has lacked the appropriate maintenance facilities to service the current fleet size. Reconstructing the facility with modern state-of-the-art technology will support a fully electric bus fleet serving routes throughout Queens, thereby eliminating carbon emissions associated with diesel fuel exhaust resulting in cleaner air for residents and customers.

Participants will be led on a tour of the work site, walking through the completed phases and the areas still under construction to get a behind-the-scenes look at how the MTA is delivering this $626 million project better, faster, and cheaper.

In early 2015, the Mother Clara Hale (MCH) Bus Depot opened for operations in New York’s Harlem neighborhood and was awarded LEED Gold certification by the US Green Building Council (USGBC) for its innovative green design and positive impact on the surrounding community, which was solicited at the outset of the project, and consistently through to the depot’s completion. 

The MCH Bus Depot includes several innovative practices that have not been widely used before by public transportation facilities. A Solar Heating Wall passive heating system is connected to the two of the rooftop air conditioning units and the depot has 30 roof top Heat Recovery Units (considered quite innovative in the industry). The MCH vegetated or green roof is the first large-size installation for MTA NYCT after a small pilot project. The depot also includes a 50,000-gallon tank to collect rainwater and use it for bus washing.

The Park Avenue Viaduct is a 133-year-old elevated structure that carries four Metro-North tracks above Park Avenue—from the Park Avenue Tunnel at East 97 Street to the Harlem River—and moves 750 trains and 260,000 passengers each day through one of New York's most constrained rail corridors. In July 2026, the MTA announced the completion of major structural work 60 months ahead of schedule and $195 million under budget. The $765 million project included the replacement of 196 bridge structures and more than 12,600 feet of railroad over 28 weekends without delaying a single train. 

This tour will be led by the Project CEO, who will give an educational walking tour along a segment of the Park Avenue Viaduct, and is best suited for engineers or architects interested in a deep dive into the technical details of this project.

Take a tour of the Club's parlors and dining room—typically only open to members—and experience the beauty of New York's Gilded Age firsthand. Marvel at the Club's historic architectural details, including the remarkable stained glass dome above the Club's bar dating from the 1880s, and see artwork from the permanent collection. sites.description:
Nevins Landing is a mixed-use development in Gowanus, Brooklyn, situated between two bridges spanning the Gowanus Canal. It comprises two towers — a taller, red-brick building and a shorter, grey building — distinguished by height and color but sharing a unified design language that references the neighborhood's industrial past, including arched details on storefronts, entryways, and windows that echo the nearby Powerhouse Arts building and other 19th-century industrial architecture in Brooklyn.

On this tour led by Harshad Pillai, Director, and Zaimee Lucca, Associate Director, from Fogarty Finger, visitors will see the architecture and interiors of the completed South Building (the grey building) at 340 Nevins Street, including its publicly accessible arcade and lobby.

An Art Deco interpretation of the Romanesque style of architecture, the academy's doors opened on November 18, 1926. NYAM is also home to one of the largest history of medicine libraries in the country, a library that has been open to the public for use since 1878.

The tour is led by Historical Collections Librarian Arlene Shaner and features the exterior, lobby, auditorium, main reading room, and the Drs. Barry and Bobbi Coller Rare Book Reading Room, where a display of materials related to the construction of the building itself and a few of the rare materials from the Library will be featured.

sites.short: Go behind the scenes with guided tours and open houses of rarely accessible science facilities, historic botanical collections, and the renowned herbarium, plus explore unique exhibitions and archival treasures with expert staff on hand.

sites.special:
**Explore the Library: **The LuEsther T. Mertz Library’s outstanding collections represent over a century of commitment to botanical and environmental research. The Mertz Library staff are proud stewards of NYBG’s rich history and invite visitors to retrace its origins through a self-guided tour of historical documentation, photographs, and ephemera. See the library exhibition, Growing America, and celebrate America’s 250th anniversary at NYBG through the plants and foods that tell the stories of American history. In the Mertz Library, see historic botanical illustrations, planting ledgers, books, and cookbooks dating from the Revolutionary War to the Victory Gardens of World War II and beyond.
- Open House: 10 AM–4 PM

**Dive Into the Herbarium Collections: **The William and Lynda Steere Herbarium at NYBG is one of the largest collections of its kind in the world, holding 7.8 million plant and fungal specimens from around the globe, and representing 250 years of botanical research. 
- **Tour at 10:30 AM: **Tour will begin on the 4th floor of the Orchid Rotunda in the Museum Building and offer a behind-the-scenes look at the treasures held in this museum of preserved plants. Visitors can see historical collections made by Charles Darwin and other scientists, learn how the collections are made, and discover their integral role in scientific research and conservation. Space is limited, first-come, first-served. 
 
**Discover the State-of-the-Art Pfizer Lab**: NYBG Science encompasses several departments and programs and includes more than one hundred scientists, including staff, graduate students, Emeritus Curators, and Adjunct Scientists. All are working toward the Garden’s scientific mission to explore, understand, and conserve Earth’s vast botanical diversity.
- **Tour at 11:30 AM:** Tour will begin in the Pfizer Laboratory lobby. Space is limited; first-come, first-served. A sign-up sheet will be available at the entrance to the Pfizer Lab 30 minutes before the start of the lab tour.

**Before New York: The Bronx Exhibition: **Before New York, there was nature. After New York, there will also be nature. Nature was, is, and forever will be a co-creator of the city we call home. The more closely we align our lives with how nature operates, the longer our city will endure and the richer and more profound our lives will become. To see the nature of the place we now call the City of New York, ecologist Dr. Eric W. Sanderson and colleagues have spent more than 25 years reconstructing lives of the inhabitants of this remarkably rich and diverse coastal landscape as it existed on September 12, 1609, on the eve of a visit by the English navigator in Dutch employ, Henry Hudson.
- **Tour at 1 PM:** Tour begins in the Ross Gallery in the Library building. Join Dr. Eric Sanderson for a tour of Before New York and learn about the plants and landscape of the Bronx as it existed 400 years ago. Space is limited; first-come, first-served.

During the tour, team members from The New York Historical and RAMSA will share insights into the building’s architectural history, its collections, and the recently completed renovation and expansion project.

sites.name: New York Marble Cemetery

address.note: Entrance between East 2nd Street and 3rd Street.

sites.description: Established in 1830, New York Marble Cemetery is the oldest nonsectarian burial ground in the city. The half-acre Greek Revival-style open space is hidden in the interior of the block, accessible through iron gates and a 100-foot private alley. The garden is surrounded by 12-foot-tall marble walls. There are no individual markers on the lawn; marble plaques in the wall name the original wealthy merchant families whose 156 underground burial chambers collectively hold the remains of more than 2,000 former New Yorkers. While the deep underground vaults are not accessible to the public, the names and occupations of the dead are all detailed in the cemetery's registers.
sites.short: Step through iron gates into a secluded 19th-century garden surrounded by marble walls, where plaques honor over 2,000 New Yorkers whose remains are interred in hidden underground vaults.

sites.name: New York Sign Museum at Noble Signs
sites.partner: New York Sign Museum and Noble Signs
sites.description:
Established in 2013, Noble Signs is a Brooklyn-based studio dedicated to the art of hand-painted and craft signage in the New York area, specifically focusing on the vernacular lettering styles that lend our city its unique visual identity. Out of that mission, the New York Sign Museum was born.

Serving as a resource for community members, historians, and designers alike, the museum is a registered nonprofit organization with the mission of preserving historic signage from around the New York metropolitan area. Currently incubating in Noble Signs’ fabrication and design studios, the museum collection includes full-scale rescued storefront signs from over 100 businesses from throughout the 20th century.

Visitors are invited to explore the collection and active sign shop where signs are still made the old-fashioned way, situated in an amazing one-of-a-kind prewar factory space. Originally built in the 1880s, 2465 Atlantic Avenue is one of the last remnants of the neighborhood as it was at the turn of the century. Updated from a hotel to a dress factory to radio equipment warehouse, details include glass block walls, Art Deco tin ceilings, stained glass dividers, and a functioning dumbwaiter.
sites.short: Explore a treasure trove of rescued hand-painted and craft signage that captures the New York area's unique visual identity, part of a museum taking shape inside a historic prewar factory with original architectural details.
sites.access_notes:
New York Sign Museum has two floors. The first floor is accessible by a small step, and a ramp is available for wheelchair users. The second floor is only accessible via a tall staircase.

Closed-toe shoes are required, as this is an active workshop. Some signs on display have flashing lights.

Luggage and non-collapsible strollers are not permitted inside the building. No pets are permitted.

The first tour, at 12 PM on Saturday, can be offered in Spanish upon request.

sites.name: New York Society Library
sites.description:
The New York Society Library, founded in 1754, is the city's oldest library and home to a thriving community of readers, writers, and families. An independent organization not connected to the city's public library systems, the Society Library is open to the public for reading, reference, exhibitions, and many events, with membership providing book circulation and use of reading/study spaces. 

The landmark building on 79th Street and Madison Avenue was built as an Italianate townhouse around 1917 and became the Library's fifth home in 1937. Tours led by the Library's Director of Programming & Communications, Sayer Holliday, with additional staff and docents, will visit public, member-only, and behind-the-scenes spaces, including elegant reading rooms, book stacks, the children’s and young adult library, and the book conservation studio. The current exhibition, Collective Witness: A Library for a Young Country, celebrates the United States’ 250th anniversary and explores how a public library and a nascent democracy converged in New York City.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes with guided tours of historic reading rooms, member-only areas, and the book conservation studio, plus view a special exhibition on the library’s role in early American democracy.
sites.access_notes:
The tours offered during OHNY Weekend require some use of stairs, in order to see historic spaces and materials. Those for whom stairs are an impediment are invited to visit at any time outside of OHNY Weekend and request a building tour.  

Visitors are asked to keep conversations at a low volume and refrain from taking any photos that might include New York Society Library patrons.

Bags larger than a standard-size backpack are not permitted. Phone calls, food, and drink are prohibited. Water bottles are allowed.

Children 9+ are welcome. Every person attending, including children, requires a ticket.

sites.name: Newtown Creek Canoeing with the North Brooklyn Community Boathouse
sites.description: Join the North Brooklyn Community Boathouse on a canoe paddle in Newtown Creek, an urban tidal estuary that forms part of the border between Brooklyn and Queens. Trained American Canoeing Association trip leaders will guide participants in 29-foot Langley canoes on a short paddle into the creek, and back out toward the East River to enjoy the views of Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens. While paddling, participants will learn about the industrial and environmental history of the creek, which remains one of the most polluted waterways in the nation and is the site of one of the largest oil spills in U.S. history. Tours are for approximately 45 minutes. Participants will be on the water for about 30 minutes, with additional time to load/unload the boats and receive paddling instruction. Along the route, participants may catch a glimpse of some wildlife (cormorants and herons are a common sight) or yield the way to a large barge!
sites.short: Paddle a 29-foot canoe through Newtown Creek with expert guides, taking in rare views of Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens while learning about the creek’s industrial legacy and local wildlife.
sites.access_notes:
Participants will be encouraged to paddle at a relaxed pace for approximately 30 minutes during the tour. The canoes have a large capacity of 10+ people per boat and so participants are able to take breaks as needed. Moderate stability and flexibility is required to access the boats, which involves stepping down a small ladder onto the dock and stepping in/out of the canoes.

Plan to arrive on time for your tour. Latecomers may not be accommodated.

Life jackets will be provided and must be worn at all times. Participants must wear close-toed shoes. Please dress appropriately for the weather (windbreaker, rain jacket, fleece, etc.), sunglasses or sun hat, and/or sunscreen. No pets are allowed on the boats.

Participants will have the option to leave personal items (i.e. backpacks, phones, keys) at our volunteer check-in table if they do not want to bring them into the canoes. 

NBCB does not have restrooms on-site so please plan ahead. 

Children under 18 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. Children participating must be able to fit into a provided life vest (sizes start at 50 pounds). All participants, including children, must have a ticket.

sites.name: Nikolas Weinstein Studios
sites.description:
Nikolas Weinstein Studios creates architecturally integrated glass sculptures that anchor and define singular projects and developments—from the studio's first project with Frank Gehry in Berlin to its most recent: the world-record-setting "Mangrove" at Solaire Resort Manila. During OHNY Weekend, visitors will learn about the tricks used to build these sometimes massive and delicate sculptures in New York and then ship them to the other side of the world to reconstruct them.

The sunlit Long Island City studio runs on a mix of disciplines that don't usually share a room: structural engineering, kiln forming, rigging, fine art, and destructive testing, alongside custom-built machines — including an exploded custom loom that makes woven glass textiles possible. The finished sculptures read as deceptively minimal, but their genesis is complex — built and designed in a studio where artists often create not just the art but all the components and technology used to bring it to life.

Visit to preview current works in progress, glimpse the studio's design and fabrication methodology, and enjoy the views of the Queensboro Bridge and the East Side skyline along the way — all from inside the Foundry, a gorgeous, singular turn-of-the-century building that spans a full city block.
sites.short: See large-scale glass sculptures in progress, explore innovative techniques and custom-built machines, and experience the creative process inside a historic, sunlit studio with sweeping city views.
sites.access_notes:
The studio is located in a historic foundry building on the second floor. There is no elevator, and access is only available by stairs. 

Closed-toe shoes are required. This is an active manufacturing environment with machinery, sharp and fragile objects, and possible fabrication debris. Visitors should avoid wearing loose clothing/accessories that may snag. No pets permitted, except for ADA service animals that can climb stairs.

Recommended for ages 12+. Children are welcome accompanied by an adult and closely supervised at all times.

The Noble Maritime Collection is an art and history museum dedicated to depicting the working waterfront of New York Harbor. The museum preserves art created by John A. See unique pieces of art, grand ship models, the personal collections of John Noble, and how all of these artifacts are preserved in the archive. A guide will lead groups through the archive to share insight and answer questions about the many curious objects and pieces of art that are with it.

sites.description:
Take part in a guided exploration of Noo Arts’ unique exhibition and performance spaces, beginning with the expansive indoor artist studio Last Frontier NYC: a working atelier and creative playground. This raw factory loft, with a Sioux-designed tepee for intimate gatherings and circus contraptions hanging from its soaring ceiling, serves as a collaborative crucible where old-school painters, avant-garde musicians, acrobats, whirling dervishes, and experimental multimedia converge.

The tour will continue to the Kingsland Wildflowers rooftop meadows three floors above. As the cultural partner in this nature sanctuary community initiative, Noo Arts activates several spectacular outdoor arenas with multidisciplinary experiences at the nexus of art and eco-awareness. 

The first half of the tour will be led by Sol Kjøk, Artist-in-Residence at Last Frontier NYC and founder of Noo Arts. The second half will be guided by Marni Majorelle, founder of Alive Structures and the visionary behind the Kingsland Wildflowers green roof project.

sites.name: Norwegian Baked Bakery at Brooklyn Army Terminal

address.note: Located in BAT Annex, 3rd floor

sites.description:
Step inside Norwegian Baked, a small-batch bakery tucked away in Sunset Park, and discover where Norwegian tradition meets Brooklyn’s food culture.

Founded in 2016 by Norwegian-born Hedvig Bourbon, Norwegian Baked grew from a Brooklyn home kitchen into a commercial bakery, bringing a modern twist to traditional Nordic crispbread—or, as Norwegian folk call it, Knekkebrød. Today, they still make each batch by hand with organic ingredients, whole grains, nutrient-rich seeds, and plenty of love and care.

During this special behind-the-scenes visit, visitors will explore the bakery and discover how crispbread goes from carefully selected ingredients to the crispy, crunchy Knekkebrød now found in specialty food stores across the country. Visitors will hear the story behind Norwegian Baked, be introduced to the craft and process of small-batch baking, and be shown the equipment and space where the magic happens.

And, of course, there will be plenty to taste! Visitors can sample their way through a full range of crispy, crunchy crispbread flavors, followed by the 2026 sofi™ Gold Award winner, KnekkeGodis — an irresistible sweet-and-salty treat made from crispbread pieces tossed in buttery caramel, crowned with fair-trade dark chocolate, and finished with cranberries and Maldon sea salt flakes. The Sea Salt Flakes Knekkebrød also received a sofi™ Silver Award in 2019 and is “Highly Recommended” by Bon Appétit.

Come have a taste and experience a little piece of Norway in Brooklyn. Found a favorite Knekkebrød during the tasting? OHNY Weekend visitors will receive a special discount to take some home!
sites.short: Go behind the scenes at a small-batch bakery to see how award-winning Norwegian crispbread is crafted by hand, sample a variety of unique flavors, and enjoy a tasting to discover a new favorite.

sites.name: NYC DDC Brooklyn Bridge-Montgomery Coastal Resilience Hard Hat Tour
sites.partner: NYC Department of Design and Construction
sites.description:
The Brooklyn Bridge-Montgomery Coastal Resilience (BMCR) project is a coastal protection initiative aimed at reducing flood risk due to coastal storms and sea level rise in the Two Bridges Neighborhood in Lower Manhattan. The BMCR project is reconstructing a portion of the East River Esplanade to reduce risk from flooding while maintaining views and waterfront access. This project will reduce flooding risk through a series of deployable flip-up barriers. These floodgates will be permanent infrastructure, hidden until they are flipped up in the event of a storm. The location of the flood walls and posts has been designed to minimize conflict with subsurface infrastructure and to maximize integration of public space amenities such as open-air seating, fitness equipment, and athletic courts. Join the NYC Department of Design and Construction (NYCDDC) and members of the construction team for a behind-the-scenes tour of the waterfront construction of BMCR, including its hidden flood protection infrastructure and future amenities.

The tour will be led by NYC DDC Associate Commissioner for Coastal Resiliency Construction Joseph Lione.
sites.short: Go behind the scenes of a major Lower Manhattan waterfront construction project to see hidden flood-protection barriers and learn how new public amenities, like open-air seating and athletic courts, are being integrated into the design.

sites.name: NYC DDC East Side Coastal Resiliency Hard Hat Tour
sites.partner: NYC Department of Design and Construction
sites.description:
The East Side Coastal Resiliency (ESCR) project is a coastal protection initiative aimed at reducing flood risk due to coastal storms and sea level rise on Manhattan's East Side from East 25th Street to Montgomery Street. The boundaries of this project correspond with the natural "pinch-points" in the 100-year floodplain: areas where the land is higher along the coastline, making it easier to close the system off from water entering from the north and south. The project design integrates flood protection into the community fabric, improving waterfront open spaces and access, rather than walling off the neighborhood.

Join the NYC Department of Design and Construction (NYC DDC) and members of the construction team for a behind-the-scenes tour of the waterfront construction of East River Park, including hidden flood protection infrastructure and completed park amenities. The tour will be led by NYC DDC Associate Commissioner for Coastal Resiliency Construction Joseph Lione.

sites.name: NYC DDC: The City Below Tour
sites.description:
Almost daily, construction crews break ground only to discover gas pipelines, fiber optic cables, or steam mains in the way of vital upgrades. These unexpected findings cost the City millions in delays and pose a threat to emergency management. To solve this problem, the City is working to create the first complete and accurate map of everything—water and sewer lines, electrical conduits, and natural gas pipelines—beneath our city’s streets. This technological feat will bring transparency to the “spaghetti-like jumble” and transform how the city builds, maintains, and protects its infrastructure.

During OHNY Weekend, join Tom Wynne, Deputy Commissioner of Infrastructure, and Amanda Amankona, Senior Strategic Planning Coordinator, from NYC Department of Design and Construction, for an up-close look at this crucial underground infrastructure. This is a perimeter tour taking place on public sidewalks adjacent to an active construction site.
sites.short: Get an in-depth look at the city’s groundbreaking effort to map every underground utility, revealing how new technology is transforming infrastructure planning and emergency response.

sites.name: NYC Department of Records & Information Services Gallery
sites.partner: NYC Department of Records & Information Services (DORIS)
sites.description:
NYC's Story: The City on Record showcases visual records from the Municipal Archives and Library collections. Selected images are arranged by borough and capture both defining events and everyday moments in New Yorkers' lives. The exhibit also premieres a new interactive map highlighting audio clips from Neighborhood Stories, an NYC Department of Records and Information Services (DORIS) storytelling initiative that gathers and permanently preserves interviews with New Yorkers. The interviews "put the community in the archives" by depicting everyday experiences that illustrate how government action, or inaction, impacts city residents.

A related interactive online exhibit featuring over 100 items from the collections within the Municipal Archives can be found at RememberNYC.nyc. Both exhibits celebrate NYC history during the 250th anniversary of the country's founding.
sites.short: Encounter personal stories from New Yorkers, brought to life through archival images, audio interviews, and an interactive map that reveal how everyday experiences and major events have shaped the city.

Participants will get an exclusive look at the systems, technologies, and teams behind NYC Ferry’s Engineering, Marine Operations, Dispatch, and Environmental departments and learn how the nation’s leading ferry system of 38 vessels carries more than 7.4 million people per year across the five boroughs while operating 365 days a year. sites.name: NYC Health Academy: A Backstage Pass to Food Safety
sites.partner: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
sites.description:
The NYC Health Department invites OHNY Weekend participants behind the scenes of New York City's food worker training center—the NYC Health Academy—where thousands of food workers learn essential food safety practices that help keep the city's restaurants, food carts, soup kitchens, school cafeterias, and other food service locations safe.

Tour participants will step inside a professional model kitchen designed to mirror a real food service environment, complete with commercial equipment, demo stations, prep areas, and the tools used every day in kitchens across the city. During the tour, participants will learn core food safety principles adapted for home cooking, including preventing cross-contamination, proper storage, and safe cooking temperatures. 

Visitors will also see how simple daily habits can protect their families from foodborne illnesses, and will walk away with practical tips they can use right away in their own kitchens. This rare look inside the Health Academy allows visitors to experience firsthand how the Health Department protects public health through education, and how every kitchen, professional or home, can be made safer with the right information.
sites.short: Learn essential food safety practices from the experts who train NYC’s food workers, with hands-on tips and a tour of a professional model kitchen designed to mirror a real food service environment.

sites.name: NYC Health: Rat Academy and Rat Walk
sites.partner: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
sites.description:
Join the NYC Health Department at the Harlem Neighborhood Health Action Center to learn about rat biology and behavior, safe and effective methods for rat prevention in the community, and what the Health Department is doing to prevent and manage rats.

Built in 1921, the Harlem Neighborhood Health Action Center is a cornerstone of the community, offering a safe and welcoming space for residents to seek services, and is a key part of the Health Department’s effort to address health equity. The Harlem Neighborhood Health Action Center houses multiple local, community-based organizations and offers a comprehensive continuum of care with services ranging from a Children’s Mental Health Clinic to adult education, legal support, financial counseling, and the Health Department’s Pest Control Services team.

After an introductory session at the Action Center, participants will head out into the neighborhood for a Rat Walk to learn where and why rats thrive by observing real neighborhood conditions. East Harlem is in the Harlem Rat Mitigation Zone, which is an area with historically high levels of neighborhood rat activity, and where the City focuses a data-driven, coordinated, multiagency effort to address rats and the conditions that cause them. Participants will learn to recognize rat conditions and effective prevention strategies and become active partners in improving neighborhood health and cleanliness. The Rat Academy session and Rat Walk will be led by NYC Health Department's Caroline Bragdon, Director of Neighborhood Interventions, Martha Vernazaa, Community Coordinator, and Jessie Lopez, Senior Neighborhood Health Manager.
sites.short: Learn about rat biology, prevention strategies, and the city's coordinated efforts to manage rats through an interactive classroom session and guided neighborhood walk led by the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene.
